utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Bakrac will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply until your evidence is completed. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If you remember last Friday, we left off analysing a document of the OSCE from the central headquarters of the OSCE in February, early March, and we saw that the OSCE assessment was that the KLA would be putting pressure on local residents to move out, and it concerned a location near the border with Macedonia. Did you have your own knowledge and evaluations or any facts, perhaps, that in other areas, too, such pressure was put on civilian population by the KLA to move out?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had both evaluations and knowledge that such things happened for a number of reasons. One reason could have been in order to move the population and to represent that as a result of the activities of Serb security forces by way of an offensive and the population was moving out in convoys. Another reason was in situations when the KLA was about to lose a piece of territory and then they would move the population and run with them. And the third reason why they moved their own population was if they thought they could stay in some villages for a longer time to use them as a stronghold from which to attack Serb security forces regularly, then they would want the population to move out so that they had the place to themselves in order to attack Serb security forces. There were many places in which that happened, not only Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, could we now look at an exhibit 5D636. Look at page 2 in B/C/S, please. Can we have page 2, please? Look at the first paragraph on page 2, item 3. It says: "KLA threat to launch large-scale actions such as new Racak or new Markale. There is information --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: "From many sources the information came in. The terrorists have six large explosive devices that they intend to use in urban environment possibly in Pristina." Two markets are being mentioned. "According to OSCE mission steps will be taken to prevent this."

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a meeting with Colonel Ciaglinski at which this was discussed. During that meeting General Loncar came in and informed us that between Nagura [phoen] and Lapovaca, a police envoy was ambushed wherein 15 policemen were wounded. Mr. Ciaglinski immediately used his cell phones and his verifiers to check this information, and he got confirmation; but General Loncar warned him that preparations were made to use six large explosive devices to be set in these places that are mentioned here. That happened in Kosovska Mitrovica, in Vucitrn, around the 13th of March, I believe. In Urosevac something happened in February, so after that meeting which happened on the 5th of February or these things happened in the second half of February, resulting in 14 or 15 deaths of local residents and a large number of wounded. So the police did not stop and did not prevent these terrorist actions, although they, and I have to emphasise this here, had their representative in the highest authorities of the so-called KLA. Both the OSCE and the American KDOM had their representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the date of this document? Can we go back to the first page, please. Yes, it's March. So it can't be predicting events in February. What you're talking about then is a meeting that you had with Colonel Ciaglinski sometime earlier than this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bonomy. I stated that because we had this knowledge back in February, and we warned the verification mission back in February, although this was done in March, this particular document. I presented this document when testifying in the Milosevic case. What I talked about now was on the 5th of February. We had knowledge back then, and we first informed the verification mission back then, although we informed them again in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I was going to ask you anyway about this. You said the verification mission did nothing to prevent this. We have also observed these tactics of moving the civilian population and creating an artificial picture of a humanitarian catastrophe. What did the verification mission do to prevent these tactics of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The task of the mission was to verify the cease-fire, see if it was being honoured, to establish freedom of movement, and to establish the person or persons responsible for every violation and offence. If the verification mission had exact knowledge that the KLA was violating the agreement on a massive scale, was launching terrorist actions, setting ambushes, kidnappings on a massive scale, they did nothing except to try to pacify us lest we took some drastic measures. They justified this by a lack of firm chain of command in the KLA and their own lack of control over certain commanders. They never made a public appearance in any media, unlike they did against us in the case of Racak. But there was nothing done by them except these declarations. I told you about Vollebaek's visit to Pristina when they said that our conduct was consistent with the situation and that we were not violating the agreement, but as far as the KLA they -- is concerned, they did nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. In the course of 1999, did you, together with Mr. Ciaglinski and Mr. Drewienkiewicz tour the state border with a view to gaining an insight into the sufficiency of troops to secure the state border?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We toured it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we have P640. This is another exhibit of the Prosecution. I would like you to look at it and to clarify for us the evaluations of the number of troops that would be sufficient to secure the state border. But before that, tell us, what was the width of the border belt?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The depth of the border belt was five kilometres, and the length of the border was 260 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was there an increase at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was increased up to ten kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You don't remember when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now please look at page 1, both in English and in Serbian -- or, rather, page 2. This is page 1. This is the cover page. In item 1 -- in item 2 we can see the length of the state border facing Albania and Macedonia, and the total length. And to move along faster, could we move to another page, the second page, for you to look at item 9. That is our evaluation. And then you could give us your comment, tell us how many men were on the state border, and then had we could look at 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15 to see the evaluations of the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We toured the border from Vrbnica in the south all the way up to Decani. That team, except Drewienkiewicz and Ciaglinski, included Mrs. Thelma Dombar [phoen] and some other people I didn't know well. Mr. Drewienkiewicz was surprised at the wildness of the border as he put it, how difficult it was to pass through and how difficult it was to secure; and he put to me a proposal that he would like to come to see me in my office the next day so that we could make a joint assessment of the number of troops to secure the state border the way we were securing it, the way we saw the problem, because that was the period when our representatives and representatives of the Albanian side were negotiating for the first time in Rambouillet. He told me that the plan put to the Serbian side envisaged that 2.000 troops would remain there to secure the state border, and he said that only they had the possibility to effect certain decisions in Rambouillet. He also said that if certain decisions are taken, they would be difficult to change later even if those decisions are bad. So we met the next day in my office, and we made this evaluation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: To move on more quickly, is it correct that your evaluation was that between 6 and 7.000 soldiers were required? And here under item 15, we see the evaluation of the KVM, 6.600 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He agreed completely with my evaluation. He had not a single objection. I explained to him why certain things were necessary, and having seen the terrain he completely agreed with my assessment. Out of -- the only little discrepancy was between 7.000 on my side and 6.600 on them, on their side. So their assessment was a couple of hundred less on the condition that these couple of hundreds would be moved to the interior of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many people were engaged actually at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 3.000. Fifty per cent of the assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kotur. Did you, with Mr. Ciaglinski, also tour Junik village and when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I toured the unit engaged in in-depth security located somewhere in Junik on the 27th or 28th of January, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we look at 5D648 briefly, and then I will ask two more questions. Was there any civilian population in Junik at the time when you visited?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was civilian population, and on our way we ran into a humanitarian organisation that was staying in Junik at the time. We struck up a conversation, and Mr. Ciaglinski participated in it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I called 5D648. Could we see page 3 in B/C/S, please. The last paragraph. It says here that on the 24th of January, from 8.30 to 0900 hours, the team leader of the Pristina Corps command and the representative of the mission, Colonel Ciaglinski visited the command of DG 125 in Junik, and then in Junik they had a conversation with a group of local Siptars.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we please scroll up a little bit. I can't see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next page now. On the page in B/C/S, that's page 4. It says here: "They talked to a group of local Siptars who say that they did not have any problems with members of the VJ." Is that this visit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the visit. I was wearing civilian clothes just like Mr. Ciaglinski. I raised this issue on purpose. I wanted Mr. Ciaglinski and the members of the humanitarian organisation to hear from the locals how the army had behaved in Junik. And I'm referring to all of 1998. I wanted them to hear whether the locals had any complaints against the army. The locals didn't know who I was. They had no idea I was an officer, and they said they had had no problems with the army in Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You said that there was civilians in Junik, civilian villagers, and that you spoke to them in January. Was Junik destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had it been destroyed, the civilians wouldn't have spoken about us the way they did. There was very little damage done to Junik when it was liberated in 1998. I think in September there was even a team of diplomats visiting Junik, and they reported that there was very little damage, to the best of my knowledge. You can see that in their report, and Ciaglinski was able to see that for himself, as was the humanitarian organisation whose representatives visited Junik with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, to expedite matters the report of the diplomats who visited Junik can be found in Exhibit P564, which is a report from the Austrian embassy, and there it's mentioned that Junik suffered little damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move on. Now that we are talking about this document, Colonel, let's take a look at page 5 of this document, which we see on the screen before us. Page 5 in B/C/S -- or, rather, I do apologise, page 3. That's the previous page. Page 3. My mistake. I apologise. Colonel, I'll read you the last sentence in the paragraph before the last. The topic of the meeting was a visit to the units of the VJ engaged in securing the state border, and it says here that it was concluded that in the border belt no movement will be allowed without prior notification and without the presence of a liaison officer. Can you tell us with whom this conclusion was reached? What does it mean when it says it was concluded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that Mr. Ciaglinski attended that meeting, and the commander of the 53rd Border Battalion and I, and that we agreed on the way the units engaged in securing the state border would be visited both on line and in-depth security; and we decided that there would have to be prior notification and that liaison officer would have to be present. It's quite logical, because the moment the mission arrived in Kosovo, we informed them of the methods of work, especially touring the units in the border belt, and the units on the ground and in barracks and special facilities. We discussed all this. And Ciaglinski fully agreed that this was the only possible manner of proceeding, and from that point on that's how we operated. Up until that moment, until January, they had developed a special method of work. This was done by Mrs. Thelma Dombar, whom I mentioned visiting the border. It was a so-called aggressive method, aggressive toward our side. They demanded access to all facilities and installations, and all units in the border belt, barracks, depots, warehouses, and this resulted in a letter being sent from Mr. Walker to Mr. Milosevic. That was not how we interpreted the agreement. If this method of work had been accepted, the possibility of securing the state border would have been nil. It would have been impossible. And the work of the Pristina Corps would have been completely paralysed because they had 1.385 verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, we have to move more quickly, so I must interrupt you. Now that we're looking at this document, could you please confirm whether -- well, we saw that on the 24th you went to Junik. Did you visit other villages, for example, Skoza, Dobriste, Vrbnica, the village of Glodjan.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We visited all those villages with this team, because it was all on the axis where the border boasts were and the border crossings. The locals were -- in Dobriste were pleased with the -- well they were satisfied with the situation. They had no complaints against the army. When asked by Mr. Drewienkiewicz what they missed or what they lacked in Dobriste they said they lacked an outpatient clinic, a health centre, and he said that he would provide aid to them to have this built. I don't know what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you wearing civilian clothes on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, we have just spoken about the way verification was carried out in the border belt. Could now take a look at Exhibit 3D787. It's a report, it seems, from the working group of the team of the General Staff of the army of Yugoslavia, and it seems -- well, let's look at this document first, and can you comment briefly on this? Could you look at the introduction, and at paragraph -- or items 1, 2, and 3. Please don't read it out loud, just comment briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this document we see that the Chief of the General Staff designated a working group of officers from the team for relations with the verification mission and NATO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 13th to the 16th of December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, could you please slow down a little. The interpreters have to pick up everything and translate it for us and you're speaking rather quickly at the moment. Thank you, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot myself for a moment. I know I had quite a lot of problems last time because of the speed of my speech. From the 13th to the 16th of December they carried out the inspection, and they saw to what extent the teams were prepared for the relations and the liaison officers from the VJ for relations with the Kosovo Verification Mission. This team established that we were fully prepared and trained to carry out the tasks set before us. That's it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, we see that in items 1, 2, and 3. Let's move to page 2 now. And it seems that in this document there is an explanation of the standpoints of the government commission of the SRJ, the FRY that is. Did you receive this explanation of the government standpoints concerning the agreement, and is that what we see here in item 5?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were already having problems with the mission, which was already in Kosovo, because of the aggressive method they had selected, and I explained what that aggressive method was. We asked for clarification from the team which had arrived from the General Staff, and they conveyed to us that the standpoints of the government commission of Yugoslavia was that there would be no entry into barracks or army facilities or verification of -- of equipment or activities or troops. The only verification allowed was that of mixed companies -- by mixed companies with prior approval and verification of VJ troops securing the in-depth security of the state border according to the protocol on verification and with previous notification; and that verification of units in the border belt would be permitted with previous notification, approval, and according to the protocol of verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, we've seen these instructions -- or, rather, this report from the General Staff and the practical guidelines issued by the FRY commission clarifying and/or interpreting the agreement. Could we now take look at 3D408. And this seems to be an order issued by the General Staff of the VJ immediately after this report of the working group. Can you tell us what this is about? Perhaps we could look at item 6 on page 2, because as we'll see later on, there was some -- something contentious about this. So could you please read the part that's underlined.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in, please? Yes. Item 6 says that: "Mission members verifiers must be treated in accordance with the status and the diplomatic immunity they have. Verification of VJ units in barracks, border posts, depots, except the PVO systems reported and stationary communications notes are not to be accepted without special approval from the VJ Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. To be implemented by the 2nd and 3rd Army commands and RV and PVO command," and that was an ongoing task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we now look at another document. That's document 3D407. And while we're waiting for the document to come up on our screens I'll put the following question to you: Did you for any reason, and we'll come to that, were you replaced from the position of team leader for the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not replaced or dismissed. There was no reason for me to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We have Exhibit 3D407 here. Again if seems to be an order, dated the 8th of March, 1999. Can you comment on this? Could you please look at the introductory part first, which shows what this is about, and then we'll move on to items 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this order -- well, it's about the organisation of work and the relations of the VJ with the OSCE and NATO verification missions in Kosovo and Metohija, and it says: "Analysing the implementation so far of the tasks deriving from the agreement on Kosovo and Metohija verification missions, it was assessed that the VJ so far had carried out its tasks from the field systematically and safely, but minor weaknesses and omissions have arisen, particularly at the tactical level, which is primarily the result of work inexperience."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me stop you now. What does it mean when it says on the tactical -- at the tactical level?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the level of brigades, liaison officers, and border battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's move to page 2, items 5 and 6 now. You don't have to read this out because we can read it for ourselves, Colonel. Just please explain the following: In item 5 it says "former combined team." Can you explain to us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 6?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, 5, yes. In the 3rd Army a combined team should be formed, because previously there had been two, the Pristina Corps team and the army command had its own team. Both teams were for relations with the Kosovo Verification Mission and each time had five members. The order now was to form a combined team comprising officers from the Pristina Corps and officers from the 3rd Army and this team should number ten people. That's it. That's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's look at the next page, and before 7 it says -- before item 7 it says -- next page, please. "Form groups of liaison officers." And then let's look at the last paragraph of item 6, just before item 7. It says in addition to --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still haven't got it. Here it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it item 7?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The last paragraph before item 7. "In addition to liaison officers specified by this order, continue engaging officers who have been acting liaison officers up to this point as assistants or deputies until the newly appointed persons become fully familiar with their duties." Well, what this means is that in the Pristina Corps a total of 26 new liaison officers arrived. These were officers who were very experienced officers. One [as interpreted] spoke English. And in all the garrisons where there had been one liaison officer previously, two liaison officers were appointed in the brigade commands and the border battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, we see here that in addition to the liaison officers specified by this order other officers were still engaged. Had you been replaced? Would this have been mentioned in this order would it have said that you had been replaced rather than continuing to work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remained a member of this mixed team, but I was no longer the team leader. A colonel from the army command was designated; and he had been intelligence officers of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When was this team set up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 10th of March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: After the 10th of March 1999, since you said that you were not replaced, you remained on the team, did you have any activities in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was engaged in a number of activities of the one of them was on the 13th of March. I was the directly responsible person at the airport, and with my presence, I ensured that the Albanian team would be able to travel to Rambouillet because there were quite a few problems. Some guarantees were sought for a liaison officer team to be placed at the airport to prevent the arrest of Hashim Thaqi because there had been an arrest for his warrant out. And on the 13th, I was already at the airport together with Ciaglinski. And on the 20th, already on the 20th, the mission withdrew from Kosovo. And I also assisted Petrovic to get acquainted with the problems because he was the head of the team, of the combined team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On page 15, line 4, the witness said that all the new officers spoke English and it says in the transcript erroneously that only one of them spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody spoke English, including General Brankovic, who had come with the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you say that after the 10th that you had activities that your engaged in. Let us look now at 5D1387, items 5 and 6 on page 2. Item 5, Colonel -- well, yes, we can see the translation now. It says here "Ciaglinski was informed that 26 new liaison officers would come to Kosovo and Metohija." And then item 6. This is a document dated the 10th of March. This is when the commission was set up -- or, rather, the new team was set up and became operational. And item 6 reads as follows: "Ciaglinski reiterated his request for new talks to be held regarding their request for opening of KVM office in the village of Planeja. Colonel Kotur expressed readiness to personally take part in these talks most probably on Saturday." So here we can see that you will be personally involved even after the 10th of March in the work of the new team, and I would just like to hear your comment. Is that correct, and were you involved in those activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, elementary courtesy would not allow me not to tell Ciaglinski that I was leaving after so many months that I worked with him that I was leaving the team, the team that I was no longer be working; and that's not what I told him. I told him just that the new officers were coming in. I told him who was the new team leader and who these officers were, and even General Drewienkiewicz held a briefing for this new team of officers in the club where we held those briefings; so they were aware of the new team leader and those officers months in advance. And I say here only that they came in, took up their posts on the 10th, that they started working on at that date, and I'm telling him that I would be participating in another activity a couple of days after that regarding the opening of their office in the village of Planeja; and as I already indicated that the Slatina airport on the 13th, I made sure that the Albanian delegation would be able to leave for Rambouillet unimpeded to attend the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, just one last question regarding your replacement. Had the essence of the whole story been that you were to be replaced? Would there be any sense in making this kind of re-organisations bringing the 26 new officers or would it have been able -- that's what Ciaglinski said. Had there been a replacement would there be this kind of a reorganisation or would there just be a new order issued?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there would be just a new order for me to be replaced from the team. I would no longer be part of the team the next day there would be a new person there. There would be no ceremony, but we believe that this -- that the Kosovo Verification Mission would continue with its work we wanted to improve our relations with them, our cooperation, because we wanted to resolve the issue of Kosovo and Metohija in a peaceful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please just slow down we're having problems with interpretation because you're speaking so fast.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected that the Kosovo problem would be solved peacefully, and that is why we reorganised this team. You can see that we had twice as many people now and new people were highly skilled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you ever show to -- to Colonel Ciaglinski in the presence of his interpreter on a map your plan of dealing with the KLA and then expelling the entire Albanian population from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never showed anything of the kind. First of all, I didn't do that because there was no such plan. I was not aware of the existence of such a plan, and I consequently could not show anything to him. Mr. Ciaglinski was just given a blank map showing the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. The scale was 1:100.000 so that we could use the same maps in order to be able to coordinate because there were some inaccuracies in reporting because we were using the wrong maps and that he was the only thing that Ciaglinski was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And who told that Ciaglinski was looking for a new map and where did this map come from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the problems that we had and all the requests that we got from the Kosovo Verification Mission were presented by me at the briefings with the corps commander. So the corps commander was aware of that. All my team members were aware of that. And when I went through some of the documents I realised at that Mr. Ciaglinski asked for another set of such maps from Colonel Marinkovic who was my deputy. He chaired this meeting in my absence and there are minutes from this meeting and he replied Kotur handed over a set of maps to you just a couple of days ago, but this was then approved from the corps command, and this was done with the knowledge of the corps commander and the entire team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, at that time and now do you speak English?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I studied German at school, so I don't speak a single word of English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now look at two or three more documents and then we will set aside the topic of the OSCE. Could we now please look at 5D650. Page 3. Would I like to have that on the screen. It's in B/C/S. Page 3. Mr. Kotur, it says in this document that as you visited the village of Dobriste that you talked to, or rather, you visited the village, the representatives of the villagers, and they said that they had no problems with the VJ personnel and the representatives of the OSCE mission expressed their satisfaction with the fact that children were able to go to school freely, but a bit further down it says that the liaison officer asked some questions to the village leader, and it says then that the villagers were moving out in fear of the VJ patrols. Ten families have already moved out of the village. There are about a hundred families in the village living abroad, mostly in Slovenia, and that's where their families moved to join them. Was there any realistic fear of the VJ patrols or, rather, did you attend this meeting? And did they have any specific complaints about the conduct of the military?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I attended this meeting. I think it was somebody from the border battalion, because they went to that village of Dobriste at least 15 times or so. This is probably a report that I received from the liaison officer of the border battalion. That would be the 55th Battalion that was deployed there. I can tell you that this was irrational fear on their part. They had no complaints in that village while I was there, complaints about the conduct of the military, and nothing had changed in the meantime and even after this time. I think that the hundred families that worked abroad, I think out of a hundred families ten took their families with them, and that was in the general atmosphere of fear that prevailed in Kosovo [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosnia], and they had a place to go. They had no specific complaints, but there was this fear of -- that's what they said. I think it was irrational fear. That was the reason why those families moved out. I don't think that they really knew why they did, so there was no real foundation for their moving out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So it was late February, early March 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What has Bosnia to do with this? We've got Bosnia in the English transcript somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Slovenia was mentioned, because it says here there are a hundred families in the village living abroad, mostly in Slovenia, and those where the families moved out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear anyone mention the word "Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll have that section of the tape listened to again and a report from CLSS on the -- what was actually said to ensure that there's no misunderstanding. Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, could we please look at the second and the third paragraphs. It appears that the village of Planeja was also visited and that the representatives of the villagers stated that they had received no threats or no pressure from the VJ to move out.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here. Escorted by the liaison officer from the 55th liaison -- from the 55th Border Battalion and a representative of the OSCE mission the Planeja village was also visited.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they had no complaints about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Part of the problem that we've just encountered could be the speed at which you are speaking. So you must make a special effort to slow down your speech, your normal speech, so that we can avoid any mistranslations which can be a real danger when the translation into English is what really matters here. So please answer that question again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. Well, I can't promise that it won't again, but I will try as much as I can to control my rate of speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur -- yes. The interpreters managed to get the answer to my previous question. We can move on. Could we please now have 5D651, Exhibit 5D651. Mr. Kotur, it appears that this is the regular weekly report dated the -- for the week from the 19th until the 25th of February. From the mission liaison team of the 3rd Army command. Could we please look at page 6 in B/C/S. That's the last paragraph. It says: "On the 25th of February, between 12 and 14.30 hours --"

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait just a minute because I don't have it on my screen yet. On the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: There was a meeting with the liaison officer from all the garrisons at the Pristina Corps command and the border battalion with the exception of the Pec garrison, and the PRK commander and the team leader from the PRK chaired the meeting. So it was you and Mr. Lazarevic. Could you please tell us what was the topic discussed at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, preparations for the work in the forthcoming period, and Mr. Lazarevic had taken over as the corps commander about a month before this meeting, and he wanted to have this meeting with me and with all the other verifiers or, rather, liaison officers who were in contact with the verifiers to analyse all the problems that existed, to note once again how important our work was; and he wanted to put some kind of a personal stamp on all that, and this is why this meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you. Could we now look at page 7, the next page, and in the last paragraph it says: The recorder -- recorded incidents are discussed here, 19 of them, and could you please tell me what time period are we talking about? In what time period did those 19 incidents occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the entire period from the arrival of the mission until the date we analysed all this. This is when those 19 incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So on the part of the Pristina Corps personnel, right from the beginning of the arrival of the mission until the 25th of February there were a total of 19 incidents. Did I understand it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking only about the Pristina Corps and our relations with the OSCE mission, not the global picture in Kosovo as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind. I think that you mentioned this, and it could be apposite to talk about that now. How many verifiers were there in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, and you can see this in the materials that you have, a total number of verifiers was 1.380 verifiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And 100 -- 1.380 verifiers and 19 incidents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now look at the kind of incidents we're talking about? Well, it says training weapons on verifiers' vehicles, escorting a unit on March: 3. Stopping at gunpoint and removing them from camp areas: 2. Unnecessary use of force: 1. Ban on verifiers first passing through unit deployment areas: 10. Searches and confiscation of items: 2. Verbal threats: 1. And can we now move to the next page, and you can comment on those incidents. It says here that on several occasions the soldiers driving in the last vehicle in the column would train their weapons. It's next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a mistake here, Mr. Bakrac. There is a mistake. It says 13 and it should read 3. So that's a mistake. Three occasions when weapons were trained on the verifiers. That's what I wanted to note.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. We have the next page here. Could you please explain to us briefly these incidents and how they occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases when motor vehicles and columns of the VJ were escorted through the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, it happened sometimes that the soldiers seated on a vehicle would turn their weapons towards the verifier vehicle behind them. This would be reported to us at daily meetings that we had with verifiers. We viewed this as a major violation, and whenever we were able to establish who exactly had done that, military steps were taken against such offenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now let's move to item (b). On several occasions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do, are there records showing the disciplinary steps taken for any of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bonomy, I don't have those records. That was within the jurisdiction of the commands of the units of offenders. They would just inform us that they had taken steps against such soldiers. I don't have records to show you, but we viewed it as a major violation for a weapon, even an empty barrel, to be turned against a verifier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, we can see that there were also some incidents involving preventing OSCE mission members to pass through the lines of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, a patrol of the Kosovo Verification Mission would be on their way to a village, and they would run into a deployment area of a combat group. The mission was unannounced, and they were not allowed to go through. They wanted to move into the battle order of the combat group without announcing themselves through the liaison officers, and they were not allowed to. There were cases when if they wanted to go into a village, they had to go through a deployment area of a unit because there were no roundabout ways and byroads. In such cases they would let us know, and we would arrange for them to pass through. These were the reasons for most of such incidents they had with our soldiers when they tried to pass through a deployment area of a unit. But it is also true that they were also aggressive in their approach, testing how firm we were in our position or just taking our pulse; or maybe they wanted to be more pushy and soften us a bit, but that was the general picture of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You have explained this incident and -- as well why it happened. But we also have an item that says "Unnecessary use of force." And we read: "On the 8th of January, attack from the 243rd Mechanised Brigade fired in the area of Donje Slapuzane." Did you investigate this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not immediately able to get any information because the unit said all their shells were in place. There were no elements, it seemed, for us to blame that unit located in Dulje, that it had fired that projectile. Only later with the verifiers went on site and when they saw the residents it turned out that this never happened. Even the verifiers were able to find out for themselves. It was an incident that didn't happen and was reported by residents. It was not the first time that something like this happened. A shell of that size could not leave no trace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there any cases where the army of Yugoslavia was blamed for even more serious incidents without any justification?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the most serious incidents we were blamed for was Racak, if that's what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were there cases in which the KLA shot at the verifiers and wounded them, whereas it was later blamed on the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened somewhere around Rznic village when the verifiers were escorting a convoy of the MUP. The KLA opened fire and wounded two verifiers -- or, rather, one verifier and one interpreter. Mr. DZ, Mr. Drewienkiewicz, said at a meeting with us that he didn't really know who exactly did it; but it's possible the army did. He wasn't assertive, but he planned a doubt. And Mr. Ciaglinski, the very next day, told me that one of his interpreters was wounded and that fire had been opened on him by the KLA. He was an experienced officer and was able to see where the bullet had come from. Later on, however, Albanians themselves, the leaders of those groups that had opened fire, admitted to it, and they also demanded that the verifiers never accompany the army or the MUP when passing through areas controlled by them. And from that time on, the verifiers indeed did not do that in areas controlled by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Was there another incidents when you were accused of having shot at a KDOM vehicle on Dulje-Suva Reka road? While you're talking about that, can we call 5D1388?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you remove this -- this one here, can I be clear about one thing you mentioned. You talked about the incident which was a lie, basically, on the 8th of January; and you say that that was later discovered to have been something that just did not happen. When was it discovered that it didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I couldn't tell you now, but I know such incidents that a tank fired a shell did not happen often, and such allegations were not often made. Ciaglinski told me in one conversation that this incident that was blamed on the army had not happened, because in the village, which they visited later and checked and spoke to residents in the village a shell had not been fired in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The timing I'm trying to be clear about. When -- when was it discovered that this did not happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you. Maybe a month or two later when the snow had thawed and they were able to get to that village, but it was a considerable time later, after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It must have been later than the 25th of February if this report relates to the period 19th --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we now see 5D1388.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So I asked you a question. Were you ever accused of having fired at a KDOM vehicle - when I say "you" I mean the Army of Yugoslavia - on the Dulje-Suva Reka road?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a very serious accusation namely that the crew of an armoured reconnaissance vehicle, so-called VBM-2, had fired over and above the verifier vehicle that was driving behind from a 14.5 millimetre machine-gun on the turret of that armoured vehicle. They filed a written complaint to police in Pristina asking for an inquiry. Since this was a very serious incident, firing from an armoured vehicle against verifiers, an inquiry was made. I took steps to make an inquiry, and I established that fire had not been opened. We filed a report to the SMIP, and we established that this vehicle went downhill towards Suva Reka and that there was an explosion from an exhaust pipe. This reply seemed ludicrous to many, and it was ordered to make a reconstruction of the incident. I performed that reconstruction. The whole thing was filmed. And a Mr. Norman, a US citizen who had filed the complaint in the first place was present during the reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Never mind. We can read this from the text.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we established for effect that it was the exhaust pipe. We made minutes in Serbian and English, signed them, handed it to him personally; and it was established that it was their mistake riding in that vehicle behind, that's how he saw it, that he was being shot at. The reconstruction showed that it was not the case and that was the end to the matter. There is a video of this whole reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could we now move away from this topic to another one. At the very beginning of your testimony yesterday, you told us that from around the 21st April, 1998, until the verification mission was set up, you were stationed at the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Last week we had the testimony of Colonel Goran Jevtovic, who was also at that command post, the forward command post, and he testified in relation to one order. Can we therefore look at Prosecution Exhibit 1427. Have a look. Tell us if this is a familiar order and tell us what you can. Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you take part in drafting it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we look at the last page, item 6. I would like to hear your comment. So this is a decision of the command of the Pristina Corps from the forward command post in Djakovica. We see initials "MK" and "GJ/GJ", signed by the then-commander of the corps, Lieutenant General Pavkovic. Item 6 says: "Combat activities shall be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was drafted at the forward command post in Djakovica in the joint agreement of the officers of the police and General Pavkovic. This document refers to the routing of Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Glodjane, Rznic, Sapka [phoen], and that broader area. In item 6 we wrote that command of those combat activities will be handled by the Joint Command for Kosovo Metohija from the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica. The initials you see at the bottom are my initials and those of Goran Jevtovic. That indicates that Colonel Lazarevic was not at the forward command post at Djakovica at the time. If he had been, his initials would be here instead of mine. My question what to write in item 6 about command, Pavkovic said to write Joint Command for the K and M from the forward command post in Djakovica, and that's what we wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Prior to that did you attend some sort of coordination meeting about these activities and between whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In order to write this document, I had to attend that agreement about the use of forces. I made notes, and he used them as a basis for this document which Pavkovic accepted in its entirety and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say agreement, you mean between whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, there was Obrad Stevanovic, I believe Vlastimir Djordjevic also known as "Rodja" was there. Some of their officers, Pavkovic, myself, Goran Jevtovic. Those were the most important I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In this -- in taking this decision on joint engagement of forces, support to the MUP forces, did any civilians take part, were any civilians present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the president of the municipality who brought us fruit, if you mean civilians only, I know very well that he brought a crate of fruit, otherwise there was no one, I mean --- else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I was referring to the process of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Civilians did not attend, and they did not have the requisite knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And when you incorporated this clause, did you know what it meant?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was always included where the MUP and VJ forces acted together coordinating their actions and supporting each other. In such cases it always said Joint Command in the documents. This would mean both the army and the MUP were participating and their activities were coordinated and were to be carried out together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now we will move on to the year 1999. We have to speed up and move along. We saw in the previous testimony that practically until the OSCE mission left on the 20th of March you worked in the team for cooperation with the OSCE mission. As of the 20th of March, until around the 10th of April, where were you in 1999? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you answer that. Just keep that in mind. Before you answer it, I think one thing we should also do is have the lines 21 to 24 of page 30 translated by CLSS listening to the tape of the answer and filing that. Thank you. Please continue with your answer to that question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you remember the question, or do I need to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no need to repeat it. Pursuant to the orders, orders of the command of the Pristina Corps, I was the leader of a group of officers. Vosic, the chief of the engineers, Pokolanski [phoen], the chief of the armoured mechanised units, and myself; our task was to visit our forces which were defending the axes leading from Macedonia to Kosovo and Metohija. We visited the 175th Infantry Brigade and the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. Our task was to establish whether they had taken up the defence positions according to plan and to see whether the situation could be improved then to reach decisions with the brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And how did it come about that you went to the forward command post in Djakovica after completing that task?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon the commander of the 243rd Mechanised Brigade informed me that I had been called up from the command post of the Pristina Corps and that I should report there immediately, that the command post was in Grmija, which is several kilometres away from Pristina. On the 10th, in the late afternoon, I managed to arrive at the command post, and there I found the army commander General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. When you say on the 10th and when you mention the command post, what month are you referring to and what command post and whose?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was in April 1999. I reported to the command post of the Pristina Corps, which was then located in the Grmija area near Pristina. Pavkovic told me that there were problems at the border with Albanian in the Kosare area and that General Lazarevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Pavkovic"] had gone there to see what the problem was about and that he was awaiting his return on the 10th in the evening; and he said that he would be giving me my tasks in that respect. General Lazarevic did return in the evening to the command post of the corps in Grmija, and he told me that the Siptar terrorist forces had taken the Kosare border post, that they had entered part of our territory, that together with the brigade commander of the 125th brigade, Colonel Zivanovic, he had looked into the situation and that an action was expected on the following day to take back Kosare. The task issued to me was to go to Zivanovic, to discuss the problem with him and help him to discuss it -- resolve it. On the 11th, I went first to Djakovica, to the forward command post there, and there I found only Lieutenant Colonel Jevtovic. That was his rank at the time. From there I went to the village of Kosare where the brigade commander was. I contacted him and continued working on solving this problem from that day onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You've given us quite a lot of detail. You say from that day on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I think we can perhaps resolve this one here. If you look at line 24 of page 32, should that in fact be a reference to Lazarevic rather than Pavkovic? I think that's the name I heard in the translation, or should we instruct or a revisal of that to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says Pavkovic told me that there was -- there were problems at the border in Kosare and then it should say Lazarevic not Pavkovic had gone there to see what that was about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, you have explained how you went there. The place where you found Jevtovic, what was its name up to that point, and after that was something else set up, and as of when and, if so, who arrived there as leader?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1998 until the first half of April, including the day I arrived there, it was called a command group. With the arrival of the chief of staff of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica, that command group was transformed into the forward command post of the corps numbering several officers headed by Colonel Veroljub - I was about to say Lazarevic - Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: As of when was the forward command post of the Pristina Corps in Djakovica set up again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think on the 13th or 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And what were the main activities of you at the forward command post in Djakovica in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This forward command post had under its command all the units located in the area of Metohija, and they were defending the axes leading from Albania to Kosovo and Metohija. These were the following units: The 549th Motorised Brigade, the 125th Motorised Brigade, the 252nd Armoured Brigade, the 60 -- no, the 672nd Reconnaissance Battalion, and I don't know whether there were others. And the task was to organise the defence against aggression from Albania to Kosovo and Metohija. That was the task of the forward command post to strengthen the defence and to assist the troops daily, to assist the units daily in resolving their problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Until when did this task continue?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until we withdrew from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija -- or, rather, until the Kumanovo Agreement was kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, I will deal with two other topics, two actions before we conclude your testimony here. Firstly, are you aware of some sort of action in the Caragoj Valley on the 27th and 28th of April 1999 and, if so, what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that action. It was carried out on the so-called -- in the so-called Reka area. It was an anti-terrorist action conducted by the MUP in -- together with the forces of the army of Yugoslavia, and this was coordinated action which went on for two days, the 27th and 28th of April, 1999. The units participating in searching the terrain were the PJP company from Djakovica, the PJP company from Prizren, and in view of the fact that the PJP unit from Pec was supposed to participate but not actually participate we provided part of the forces to search that terrain from the VJ; and the units that participating were the military police company of the 52nd Military Police Battalion and a unit, a small unit, of the 63rd Parachute Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How many men in total when you mentioned these two units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were two military police platoons. Between 30 and 40, plus another 30 or 40 from the Parachute Brigade. So the numbers were equivalent to the MUP company from Pec, which was supposed to participate but did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you participate in some sort of coordination? Were there any discussions before this action and with whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on behalf of the forward command post I participated in agreeing and coordinating this action with the chief of the secretariat of the MUP in Djakovica, Police Colonel Kovacevic. In the working agreement, he said -- or, rather, in that meeting to coordinate, he said that they lacked men because of this Pec company, which would not participate. So we were able to provide those two small units. And he asked me to have these two units be active on the Dobros-Ramoc axis, which was in a wooded area in the most difficult terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now that we're discussing this, you say that some units were holding the blockade. Can you tell us who was in the blockade and what the strength was of these units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Reka area is bounded by the Junik-Bunosevac-Djakovica road. It's a road running parallel to the border some four or five kilometres distant from the border in the depth of our territory. All our units defending this axis Cafa Prusa, Morina, Kosare, in the depth of their defence positions they relied on that road. That was all in the area known as Reka. Another part of the Reka area is bounded by the Pec-Djakovica road, but parallel to that road there is a big ridge, the Cabrisko [phoen] ridge, and another ridge with no name with several elevated points about 400 metres. That was the trig point. And in the course of this anti-terrorist action conducted by the MUP in coordination -- in coordinated action with the Pristina Corps forces, all the troops stationed near Reka received the order that with part of their forces they should secure the axis from Reka and not permit infiltration of terrorist forces into their order of battle. There were about 200 terrorist in the Bila area. It was their 137th Terrorist Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say to secure and how, what was the strength of those forces holding the blockade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were holding their part of the battle order in that and only a small part of their unit was turned around to face Reka in order to prevent infiltration of terrorist forces into their battle order, and this was -- well, I couldn't tell you the numbers now, but I know that the 2nd Motorised Battalion of the 549th Brigade, which was defending the Cafa Pruse-Djakovica access used part of their forces to -- for security in the direction of Korenica, perhaps one or two platoons. The 549th [as interpreted] Brigade defending the Morina-Kosare axis also used part of their forces for security from Smonica further on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, just to check that I understand you properly, what brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 125th. Well, it's erroneous reason us in the transcript. It says 549th and should be 125th. Also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down and could the counsel and witness please refrain from overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've lost our -- a match between you speaking and the translation again for two reasons. One is again the speed at which you're speaking, and the other is the failure of Mr. Bakrac to pause between your answer and his question. So if you could remember to just generally go more slowly. We will make more progress as it turns out, so please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, we lost -- we got in what you said about the 125th, but could you please repeat the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade and where it was and what kind of personnel -- the personnel numbers that they had. That was an air defence brigade.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 52nd Air Defence Artillery Rocket Brigade had about two platoons. So 30 to 40 men in total to man the Kosa Cavrat positions in order to prevent the infiltration of the terrorist forces at the Cavratska Kosa ridge and towards Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. As for the section that you just told us about, did the Pristina Corps forward command post or the Pristina Corps, did any of them draft a written decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You just told us what was agreed at a coordination meeting. Who did you convey that to, and who was actually -- who did actually convey this order to the units that were -- that had set up this blockade and that carried out all those activities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Veroljub Zivanovic [as interpreted] Issued a task to the units to take up or to secure from the Reka axis. You see, the units at platoon and company level are not issued a written order. In a war, command is exercised through issuing brief command -- combat commands. Zivkovic could not have issued an order in any other way but by calling the commander of another brigade, and this other battalion of the 549th Brigade, and to issue an order to them and to tell them that on the 27th and the 28th of April there would be an anti-terrorist action carried out by the MUP forces in the Reka valley, the objective of which was to rout the terrorist forces located there. To that end, you must secure your positions from the Reka axis, and then perhaps specific orders would be issued to the 2nd Battalion in the Korenica sector and to tell the commander of the 125th Motorised Brigade from the region of Smonica and above and also the orders to the people in Cabrat to prevent the infiltration of the terrorist forces into their battle order. This was all he was supposed to give them to tell them and that's what he did. All the rest was up to the unit commanders they were to designate the appropriate forces and exercise command of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be a convenient time for the break but I would like us to just correct what it says at page 38, line 19. It says Zivanovic, and in fact it was Colonel Zivkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We have to break at this stage, Mr. Kotur. That break will be for about half an hour. While that's happening could you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher, and we'll see you at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us continue where we stopped. We were talking about the 27th and the 28th of April. My next question is did the corps commander, Mr. Lazarevic, was he in Djakovica on the 27th and the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Had he been in Djakovica would you known that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have known that, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were on the 27th and the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th and the 28th I was in the 125th Motorised Brigade for most of the day. On the 27th, in the afternoon, I was at Cavratska Kosa ridge [Realtime transcript read in error "village"] for maybe 10 minutes with the company commander, the commander of the PJP unit from Djakovica, Lieutenant Colonel Colic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The fact that you spent some 20 minutes at the Cavratska plateau was that on the 27th, the first day or the second day the 28th?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 28th, the second day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Captain Nike Peraj?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you change on to that subject, it's a very unclear answer at line 9 onwards, Mr. Bakrac. First of all, the witness says that it was the 27th he was at the Cavratska village and then you have that corrected to the 28th. Well, where was he the rest of the time? Was he with the 125th the whole time or -- just ask that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the transcript should read ridge not village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, let me reformulate the question. Can you tell me, Colonel, where you were on the 27th of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th of April I was in the sector of the 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And on the 28th where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 28th I spent most of the day with the 125th Motorised Brigade and in the morning I spent maybe some 20 minutes at the Cavratska Kosa ridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say Cavratska Kosa ridge is it close to the location called Osehilja or where is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is actually facing the village of Osehilja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know Captain Nike Peraj?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Captain Nike Peraj by sight, very superficially.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, Nike Peraj testified before this Trial Chamber, and he also gave some written statements. In his evidence he claims that in the field at Osehilja you together with Novica Stankovic from the Djakovica Brigade, as he put it, represented the command in this action and that the action was controlled by Lazarevic with Jevtic from the forward command post in Djakovica. Are these claimed made by Witness Peraj correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The claims made by Witness Nike Peraj are completely inaccurate. They have nothing to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you yourself see Witness Nike Peraj on the 28th of April?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Witness Nike Peraj at Cavratska Kosa ridge only the 28th when he arrived with Mr. Perovic, captain in the VJ army. That was his rank at the time. And they said that they had come -- that Peraj had come to see his house to see what condition it was. He had a house in the village of Doso or Dolos. I didn't know where he house was but from then on I did know that it was in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It was possible to see the Caragoj or the Reka valley from that location?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see a part of the Reka valley from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Would it be possible to see from that location whether any houses had been set on fire in the Reka valley?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there at the ridge no house was on fire, and it was impossible to see anything burning on the 28th in that time that I spent there at the ridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: How long did Nike Peraj remain there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there for maybe just a few minutes after Peraj's arrival and then I left so that I can't tell you how long Peraj -- for how long Peraj was there because I did not come back to that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At Osehilja where you said that you were during those 20 minutes was there a military command post or observation post set up there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Osehilja I found the chief of staff of the 52nd air defence Rocket Artillery Brigade Lieutenant Colonel Stankovic, who was there visiting his soldiers who were -- had set up the blockade in that sector in the Reka valley. So there was no command post there. For a command post to exist, first you have to dig up the observation post, the trenches, the roads. Somebody would be there controlling this action there at the observation post with appropriate equipment, communications and observation equipment with his security. So that would be a large group of people, and it would be impossible to reach this observation post. One couldn't just walk into this observation post and say, "Well, here I am at this observation post," as Peraj did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Colonel, Nike Peraj, it is in his first statement dated 2000, year 2000, makes no mention of having seen General Lazarevic at the forward command post in Djakovica on the 27th and the 28th. Apparently he recalled that at a later stage. But he said that Micunovic, Kovacevic, and Kotur were responsible for Meja and Korenica and that they had planned the whole operation. Are these claims by Witness -- is these claims made by Nike Peraj correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those claims made by Nike Peraj are not correct. I recounted a little while ago how the Reka operation developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, the same witness says that you, Jevtovic, and Lazarevic in Djakovica went to attend daily meetings at 8.00 in the morning and 6.00 p.m. with Stanojevic, the mayor; Micunovic, the commander of a platoon; Samovic, the intelligence chief; Adamovic, the MUP chief; and the commander of the 22nd Air Defence Rocket and Artillery Brigade Djosa. Are these claims correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meetings of this kind attended by those people were not held. We from the VJ went to see the MUP people only when we were invited by them or perhaps we would invite them if there was any need for us to discuss some particular issue, but there were no regular daily meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you say "we," who do you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Peraj claims that up until that time, so that would be around the 27th and the 28th of April, because he's describing this event, that General Lazarevic spent most of his time in Djakovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lazarevic was in Djakovica on the 10th -- or, rather, he -- when he was in the 122nd [as interpreted] Motorised Brigade because of Kosare, I think he maybe just passed through once or twice, but that's all. He did not, definitely did not spend most of his time in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Witness Peraj -- Witness Peraj also says -- there is an error in the transcript. It should -- it should read 125th Motorised Brigade, and the rest has been corrected. So it's just 125th Brigade. Colonel, Witness Peraj claims that on the 28th, in the morning of the 28th, before he came to Osehilja he went to the forward command post in Djakovica and from Lazarevic and Jevtovic he was given approval to going to Ramoc and they conveyed this approval had been given to him to you. Are these claims correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those claims made by Nike Peraj are not correct because Lazarevic was not in Djakovica and he could not have conveyed anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you have any communications with the forward command post on the 28th of April from that location at Cabrat?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any communications with the forward command post from Cabrat and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is Ramoc where the home of Peraj had been or was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to explain. The Peraj home was located in the village of Dolosaj and Ramoc is the whole area. There is a village of Ramoc, but as the witness has explained to me, it also includes a broader region, and Peraj in his testimony said that he had asked permission to go to Ramoc and that he was given this approval. That's why I phrased this question in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, how was it you knew that -- that Peraj had been permitted to visit his home -- or was there to visit his home?
