utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I didn't know whether he had been given this approval or not. He came to join his unit, because the 52nd Rocket and Artillery Brigade was stationed there, and he was an officer from that unit. He went to that location where Lieutenant Colonel Novica Stankovic, his superior officer was. I just happened to be there with the commander of the PJP unit, Colic. So I don't know whether he had been given an approval or not, but he didn't need any approval to go to that location that he actually reached, because his own unit was stationed there and he was accompanied by a security officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us again how it was you knew that he was going to see his house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. I didn't say that I had known that he would go and visit his home. I only said that when they came they said that they had come to see whether his house was whole, whether that it had been set on fire or something like that. That's the only thing that I said. And we told him that there was no fire, no houses had been set on fire, and the unit had already gone through his village as part of the search operation, and we told him it had not been set on fire because we would have seen that. That's what we talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just to make everything completely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This ridge is above this village. So what would be the distance as the crow flies between Osehilja and the ridge itself to Captain Peraj's house?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately one kilometre, but I have a map of this area and I can bring this map during our next break and then perhaps it would be much clearer to all of us the size of the area. It's a blank map. The scale is 1:50.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And finally, Colonel, Peraj stated talking about you that he knew that you, Kovacevic and Micunovic in May 1999 had carried out some kind of operation at Cabrat where a certain number of civilians had been killed. He was unable to provide any details about this action. This is the only thing he said could you now tell me whether there is any truth in what he said?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take part in that operation and I'm not aware of it. All I know is that the 52nd Artillery Brigade had certain losses at this Cabrat feature, but who participated. If anyone participated, if any action had been planned, I don't know in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And my last topic has to do with two documents and that will exhaust all my questions. It's about the action called Sekac or Chisel. Can we have up on e-court P2011. While we're waiting, are you familiar with the order to smash the Siptar terrorist forces in the lake Radonjic area, so-called Chisel action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that order to smash Siptar terrorist forces in the area of lake Radonjic called Chisel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you entitled to sign that order and, if so, on whose instruction? We could look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the forward command post, Colonel Zivanovic -- sorry, Zivkovic, authorised this action, and on his authority I signed this document, because he was not there at the time and the document needed to be signed in order to be forwarded to units for them to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We see here in the decision -- or, rather, order that tasks are clearly indicated for some MUP units too. Was MUP resubordinated to you, and why does this order include tasks for the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP was not subordinated to us, and the tasks indicated for MUP units, well, in every an action in which police forces were engaged together with army forces their tasks are written together. We saw recently a document to crush terrorist forces near Prilep and Glodjane, and there, too, we had tasks indicated for army units and MUP units near Pec. It was signed by Pavkovic. We saw that in the first part of this examination, because units that participate together cannot not know who has which task. Such a task would be impossible to carry out if we bear in mind those were live bullets, there was danger of friendly fire, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was this action, Chisel, complicated, and how long did it take?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This action was complicated by the very fact that we did not have sufficient forces to execute it in one move, in one go. Therefore, it was planned to be carried out in three stages with frequent regrouping of forces. If you read the order, you will notice that. And in such a complex operation detailed tasks needed to be formulated for the forces involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. How long did the operation -- this action last?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was supposed to be over within a few days, but it lasted all of 14 or 15 days, and it was not quite completed. About 50 per cent of the plan was carried out, because already in end May and early June there was some indications that a truce will be signed, some sort of plan, that airstrikes would stop, and the units engaged in that action were affected by lethargy, apathy. Their overwhelming desire was to survive, to see the end of that action. So the action lasted longer than planned, and it was not carried out as planned, not completely, because there was an impending agreement and we stopped the action a couple of days before the planned termination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 5D227? That's a combat report from the command of the Pristina Corps, dated 20th May, and in item 2 on page 2 could you just tell us about one sentence. Item 2, at 2.2 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Below the words "125th Brigade." At the forward command post on the 19th of May, there was a working meeting --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At the forward command post of the Pristina Corps, on 19 May there was a working meeting with the MUP with a view to executing an action to route the Siptar terrorist forces in the broader area of Jablanica village.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was good and then it was moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we have the previous page? It was appropriately zoomed in at the right passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we were supposed to have the translation for this by now but it hasn't. We will let you know as soon as it arrives.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Therefore, could you please read this sentence and explain briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph, because you did according to the transcript say 2.2 and that's why the page was turned. Which page -- which paragraph should we be looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 2.1. The third bullet point. It says: "At the forward command post of the Pristina Corps". So there's a general paragraph and then bullet points. The third bullet point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read this out. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Read that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the forward command post of the Pristina Corps on 19 May a meeting -- a working meeting with the MUP was held for the purpose of carrying out actions to destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the broader area of Lake Radonjic and Jablanica village."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's enough. Is that in relation to this action, and what kind of working meeting was it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a meeting between representatives of the MUP and us on the eve of an action that was to be carried out in the area of Lake Radonjic and Jablanica village under the name of Chisel, Sekac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that the coordination with MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. Let me see. Yes, that's it Lake Radonjic and Jablanica village. That's the action, Chisel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question and last document, Mr. Kotur, is Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour. There's some error. Your Honour, 5D1382. Page 2, please. Page 2 in B/C/S. Page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you please read and explain this paragraph at the top. "In the course of the day, preparations --"

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the course of the day, preparations for action Chisel (destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Jablanica village and Lake Radonjic), readiness on 23rd May 1999 at 0500 hours. Action to be led by Colonel Milan Kotur with the chief of SUP Djakovica. Observation post on Suka Vogelj feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see the action was to be led by Colonel Milan Kotur with the chief of SUP Djakovica. You led whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I commanded the units of the army of Yugoslavia in that action, and Colonel Kovacevic commanded MUP units, and that is why in this document I did not write "Joint Command" or anything like that. I wrote "the action shall be led by," because it was a joint action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those were all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will have a few questions, and they do not regard the Joint Command, believe it or not. [In English] Surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kotur, did you have any knowledge that NATO was planning an evacuation, that is a pull-out of the members of the KVM from Kosovo in your time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that the NATO was planning and envisioning an action to pull out the Kosovo Verification Mission and for that purpose they had grouped forces in the territory of Macedonia. We learned that from our intelligence and security organs and service, and I had the same information from Mr. Ciaglinski.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you know that NATO officers entered and moved around the territory of Kosovo under the auspices of the Kosovo Verification Mission and with their documents?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that, too, that NATO officers moved around Kosovo and Metohija under the auspices of the -- or under the cover of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ciaglinski with whom you had frequent contacts tell you something about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that Ciaglinski was a NATO officer himself, Drewienkiewicz too. The officers in Kosovo -- Kosovska Mitrovica were French officers, but they were part of NATO units. And I know that sometime in the second half of February Mr. Ciaglinski went to report to the NATO command in Brussels about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija. So he didn't go to reports to the OSCE in Vienna where the mission he represented was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you now look at 2D392. I provided this document, Your Honours, to my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, and he agreed to the use of this document. It is not helpful to the Prosecution or the Defence. It is helpful to you, because there has been a lot of talk about the relationship between NATO and the OSCE, and this document reflects this aspect. It's correspondence between the NATO and the OSCE. I don't think it works either for my case or the Prosecution case. So look at document 2D392. On page 1 you see that it is an exchange of letters between the Secretary-General of the OSCE, Mr. Aragona and the General-Secretary of NATO, Mr. Solana; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, could you please look -- those were letters of the 4th of November 1998 at the very beginning of the mission could you look at page 5, please in e-court in English and page 3 in Serbian. I would like to call these pages on e-court. Could we zoom in, please. The last paragraph in Serbian. And in English we need page 5. The Serbian side is good. The English is not. Page 5. This is not 5. Page 5 in English. That is the paragraph. It's the last paragraph in both versions. Could you also enlarge the last paragraph in Serbian so that the Colonel can see it. I don't speak B/C/S, I speak Serbian. Do you see this sentence? That's Javier Solana saying -- will you read it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean this, "You will be aware"?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You will be aware the North Atlantic Council has commissioned work on the separate question of possible arrangements for NATO assistance in the extraction/evacuation of the OSCE Verification Mission from Kosovo. The results of this work will be communicated to OSCE as soon as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now look at this same document. English page 7 -- document 2D392. It's annex, in English, 7, and 4 in Serbian. Can we take a look -- let's just have the Serbian version, and can we zoom into the paragraph before the last. There, that one. No, no, no down. Further down. It starts with the words, "Conditions will be put in place." Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Conditions will be created for the setting up of reliable communication --"

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, no. Lower down.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Conditions will be created for -- to make possible any necessary travel by NATO employees from the proposed verification coordination body in Skopje into Kosovo. Whether (to the OSCE mission headquarters Pristina or elsewhere), to take place under OSCE mission status. Likewise arrangements should be made to facilitate any necessary travel to Skopje by OSCE personnel from Pristina."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I wanted. Does this correspond to what you saw when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponds to what we knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, Kostic, my name is Dan Ivetic, and I'm the counsel for Sreten Lukic in these proceedings so I have a questions for you today. First of all I would like to ask you about your time period in 1998 with the KVM mission. During your time as liaison officer for the VJ with the KVM. I'm sure that you had opportunity to come into contact with Colonel Miroslav Mijatovic of the Serbian MUP, who was the liaison from the MUP side with the KVM. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And based on your encounters with Colonel Mijatovic, would you assess him as working cooperatively with yourself and others in the meetings with the mission?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mijatovic was cooperative, but he defended his standpoints, and I think rightly. He defended them very persistently at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, and the reason I paused is I'm waiting for the English translation and the transcript to catch up with me; so please don't take it personally if I seem to not respond immediately to one of your answers. Now, I'd like to ask you about a couple of things that -- that General Drewienkiewicz represented here. First of all, was General Drewienkiewicz correct that you had the opinion that the methods of the Serbian police were tyrannical in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me try and rephrase it for you then, sir. General Drewienkiewicz, in his sworn testimony here, claimed that you, yourself, were of the opinion that the Serbian MUP in Kosovo and Metohija was tyrannical. Do you agree with General Drewienkiewicz's representation of your conclusions about the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a complete falsehood. I never thought anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Furthermore, General Drewienkiewicz said that at one particular meeting when discussing Podujevo after there had been some sort of disagreement and General Loncar had been kicked out of the meeting by the KVM members, that you were quoted --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we have a page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This should be at page -- pardon me. Let me take a step back, P2508, the sworn statement of General Drewienkiewicz, at page 19 of the Serbian and page 17 of the English claims that during this meeting where General Loncar was kicked out of the meeting by the representatives of the KVM that you said these words, Colonel, "Police, you can't trust them." Did you in fact utter such disparaging remarks about the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that anyone could have thrown General Loncar out of a meeting he was attending and let me, who was his assistant, remain. There would be no logic in kicking out Loncar and leaving Kotur there. And secondly I never said this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Your Honour. I think the statement, as I read it, General DZ is saying that this is what Walker said that Kotur said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's why I think I phrased my question did you in fact utter such remarks about the police rather than whether he agreed with the assessment of -- of DZ or Walker or et cetera. I think the question and the answer are clear if -- if -- if there's anything else that needs to be touched on that fact I would be happy to explore it, but I thought I was rather clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The evidence is clear but the question is did you agree with General DZ's representation of your conclusions about the Serbian MUP. However, it's simply been clarified by what Mr. Hannis has said and you didn't need to go back over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you testified about the activities around the 27th and the 28th of April, 1999, in the Djakovica region, specifically the Caragoj or the Reka valley. Now we've heard from other VJ officers stating that this region, the Caragoj or Reka region was within the extended border belt. Would you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether at the time the border belt had already been extended. That's one thing. And secondly, war had already started, so there was no longer any border belt or border units or border lines. There were brigades given the task of defending certain axes. They took up their areas, and in their areas or zones they were responsible. So there was no longer any border belt or five or ten kilometres. Once the war broke out, the situation was no longer the same as it had been in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, would I be correct then to say that this region was within the zone of defence, that is to say the "zona odbrana," and also the area of allocation,"rejoni rasporeda," of units of the army of Yugoslavia in the tail end of April, 1999, specifically April 27th and 28th, 1999?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does it not follow from what the witness has just said that the whole of Kosovo would be in -- in fact, the whole of Serbia would be within the zone of defence of the army of Yugoslavia by April?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking for clarification, Your Honour, based on evidence we've had from other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, would it then follow that the Caragoj or Reka region would be within the zone of defence or the areas of allocation of units of the VJ at the relevant time period, around the 27th, 28th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to clarify something here, because I see it's insufficiently clear. When a state of war is declared, then there are no longer any border units. There are no longer the zones we had before, border belts and so on. That's quite normal. A unit waging war in the area takes up position in that area. There are no longer any border lines or border belts. A unit is given a zone to defend on the ground. Where this terrorist was or anti-terrorist group of the 137th Brigade in the Reka area, Reka was between two positions, between units. There was a gap. It was between the units north of the Junik-Korenica-Djakovica road, and in depth this zone of defence was adjacent to that communication. From that communication onwards, there was the area called Reka and its depth was up to the communication going from a road going Pec to Djakovica. So that was a gap between two defence sectors of the army of Yugoslavia just as Jablanica was another such area much it was not take up by the army. It was a gap between our units in the order of battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Again waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. Now this action that took place the 27th and the 28th of April 1999, this legitimate action aimed at the terrorists of the 137th Brigade in the Reka area, am I correct that this was a joint action between -- or with the VJ and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in essence it was a MUP action. Only part of the forces engaged there belonged to the VJ. When I say part, I mean only those forces which were directly involved in the search and mopping up of the terrain. All the other units engaged there were there to protect their battle order, in order to prevent the infiltration of terrorist forces from the Reka area into their battle order. So they were not involved, and that's why they are not listed by name as participating. So that is a task to the units to make sure they were secure from infiltration from the Reka area and to make sure that there was no infiltration of terrorists from the Reka area into their areas of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now, with respect to these forces, based upon what principle, rule or other modus operandi could the MUP lead and be in charge of an action where VJ units are being utilised, or was, in fact, the VJ commander in charge of activities of both these units in their area of deployment and those that were directly involved in the search and mopping up of the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was a MUP action. One of their task was to fight the terrorist forces in Kosovo, and according to the number of forces engaged and their combat deployment one can see that the -- there were police forces intended for that fight at company level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was asking you to focus upon the units of the VJ that were involved either in the search and mopping up of the terrain or who had been deployed in their areas of deployment and were part of the blockade, I think it said. Were these units operating under the command of the MUP? And if not, who was commanding these VJ forces?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were securing their own positions to prevent a spill-over of forces from the area of Reka into their area in that combat disposition there were units that were command by their own unit commanders. On the other hand, a part of the forces that were engaged in the search of the terrain were under the command, I believe, of the commander of the 63rd Parachute Brigade. I mean that platoon from the Parachute Brigade and another unit that was with -- The MUP forces were under the command of police commanders, and army units were commanded by army commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned coordination with Colonel Kovacevic of the Djakovica SUP with respect to this -- this action or these actions, as it were. On whose initiative and upon whose order or authorisation did you meet with Colonel Kovacevic for this coordination?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to every coordination with Colonel Kovacevic on the orders of the commander of the forward command post, that is chief of staff of the Pristina Corps, Colonel Zivkovic, Veroljub. I was his subordinate. He was my immediate superior. On my own accord I could not do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during the course of this coordination was there any map created or utilised to show the locations and/or directions of troops that were to be utilised or forces, that were to be utilised in this action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had used the map in order to be able to see all the axes of movement, which unit will be where and what.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Kotur, you will now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us when you first joined the army? What year was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20th July 1970 was when I joined the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: March 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you first attain the rank of colonel?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what led you to retire in 2004? I see that's 30 plus years but it's not quite 35. Was there any particular reason you resigned in that year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no particular reason. I had almost 42 years of pensionable service and 52 years of age, and on top of that a reorganisation of the army started in 2001. Even 59-year-old men were retired, let alone me who was born in 1947. Under the law in force then, one went into retirement with 57 years of age and a full service age of 40. I was to be 57 in September, and I was retired on the 31st of March of the same year, just six months before my 57th birthday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You told us that you had the position of chief of infantry. When did you first become chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps I became in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the -- what's the role or what are the duties of the chief of infantry in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All chiefs of arms, including infantry, have as a basic duty to know the exact status and to control the exact status of their units, readiness, training, mobility, level of equipment, any problems with the troops, et cetera. Every chief of arm was responsible for that, and those were the most professional organs within the units with which they work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you -- where did you fit in the chain of command then in the Pristina Corps? I know you just told us that the chief of staff or deputy commander in 1999 was your immediate superior, but who's -- who's beneath you. Are you in the chain of command vis-a-vis the brigade commanders or are you somewhere to the side? How does that work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were professional organs of the chief of staff and we were directly linked to the chief of staff. When I say "we," I mean all chiefs of arms, be it engineers, communications, infantry, or the chief of armoured units. We were directly connected with the chief of staff. We don't have a single subordinate below us. We are in the staff headquarters, and in the hierarchy we don't have a single subordinate below us, not even a clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you got that position? Were you appointed by the commander? How -- how did you become the chief of infantry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became chief of infantry by virtue of an order from the chief of General Staff. I believe it was his authority to issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that General Perisic at the time? I think you said it was 1994.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. General Perisic was chief of General Staff, and it was his order on my appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to skip to something different now. We were talking about when you were working with the KVM. As about the 10th of March when these new personnel were brought on and you understand there's been some discussion about -- Ciaglinski says you were replaced, you say you weren't replaced. How did your duties change after the 10th of March. Before, you'd been Loncar's assistant and head of a team. What changed then when the new people came on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those new people came, what changed was that General Loncar remained in his position. Instead of his assistant for military issues, earlier me, Mr. Brankovic came to assist Loncar. And instead of the army team that before this reorganisation was led by General Mladenovic, with assistant Colonel Sredojevic, and you can see that from all the documents that the command of the 3rd Army sent to the General Staff, you will see Mladenovic head of the army team or Sredojevic in his absence. I was heading the Pristina team. Now, the reorganisation created a mixed team headed by Colonel Petrovic. He was chief of the intelligence department in the 3rd Army. It was from that position that he came to the new one. General Mladenovic was no longer on the team. Colonel Sredojevic was no longer on the team, but I remained on the team from the Pristina Corps which now about 10 people instead of five and I kept my position as chief of infantry. That did not stop. My job vis-a-vis the verification mission had priority over my duties as chief of infantry that's the only thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us on direct earlier this morning that after the 10th of March one of the things that you did in connection with the -- with the KVM and the OSCE was helping make sure the Albanian delegation got on the plane safely on, I think you said, the 13th of March; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Prior to the 10th of March I understood from other evidence that you attended meetings with -- with the OSCE on a regular basis. A daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after the 10th of March and until the mission left on the 20th of March, how many meetings did you attend with the OSCE representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period I did not attend meetings with the verification mission except for a meeting that I had with Ciaglinski at the Slatina airport as we were jointly seeing their delegation off, if you can call that a joint activity. But the point was that these meetings were attended by Loncar and his assistant. Now, General Brankovic was there, so I was not attending those meetings any longer. And as for my daily meetings with Ciaglinski at 10.00 a.m., that used to be a regular meeting, and sometimes we met several times a day, at that meeting as head of team I chaired the meeting. I had one secretary and one interpreter. So it was not usual for any other members of my team to take part because all of us had our respective duties apart from the ones linked to the verification mission. So when the new mixed team was created headed by Colonel Petrovic, he went to those meetings and I no longer needed to, nor was it the practice. And Brankovic replaced me as assistant of Loncar, so I had neither the need nor the possibility to do that. Training had been done. They knew that job very well by that time, and even General Drewienkiewicz held a lecture for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, based -- I mean, Colonel, based on that you can see where Colonel Ciaglinski may have viewed the change in circumstances as you being replaced, because Brankovic is now Loncar's assistant and you aren't attending any of the meetings, the ones with Loncar or the daily meetings you used to have with Ciaglinski. And you can see how he might characterise that as a replacement, can't you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Looking at his statement I can see that, but I don't see in reality a single moment that would make him think so, because we met on the 10th. There is a complete record of that meeting taken by an officer from the federal Foreign Ministry, and it was signed by his chief Solana. So there is nothing evidence unsaid or unclear. And he knew Brankovic was coming and he knew about all those changes. He knew there was no army team any longer, so I don't know how I came to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Something I had a question about, you said in one of your answers earlier today that they had known, meaning Ciaglinski and General DZ, that they had known for months that the replacements were coming. When -- when were they first advised of that prior to the 9th or 10th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he didn't know for months in advance, but they knew for a month before. And there was a course that they even led. DZ conducted that training. Ciaglinski was there. We told them that new officers were coming who speak English. That would be the only job they would have in our units, to be liaison officers. We were trying to improve our work, because we had noticed that on level -- lower levels, in border battalions and brigades there had been mistakes made and problems, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two things. I'll try to ask lots of questions that just require short answers, and again you're probably talking too quickly for the interpreters. Now, do you recall -- you testified in the Slobodan Milosevic trial in January 2006. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of the transcript in your language, but since you testified have you ever had a chance to review the evidence you gave in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed it once, read it like a novel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the things that you were asked about was your -- your role in the Pristina Corps, and at page 47872 [sic] of the transcript on 24 January 2006, you mentioned that you were only a member of the command that executed its missions, and you said: "I was never in such a place in the chain of command that would give me the opportunity to command." But that's not correct, is it, because we've just seen with your -- with Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Ivetic, Exhibit P2011, which is the 20 May order for operation Sekac or Chisel where you signed that, and we've seen the related exhibit 5D1382 from the 22nd of May, 1999, which indicates that you, along with the police commander, are going to command the action. So at least on that one occasion you had the authority to command in 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right when you're saying about this action that I was given authority to lead it as far as the army of Yugoslavia is concerned, but I did it on the authority, on the orders of the chief of staff, the commander of the forward command post who authorised me to do that. Otherwise, according to establishment, I had no right to issue orders to units, to issue them with tasks, nor were they obliged to obey my orders. Everybody knew that. I had no command responsibility. I would have had command responsibility if I had been a brigade commander, but not being who I was, chief of the arm of infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on page 47483, the next page, you said: "As for deciding how the units would be used, that was never my role." But for operation Sekac, you and Kovacevic decided how the units were being to be used, didn't you, in your coordination meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, decision-making is one thing, and it's quite different from debate and agreement. The commander is the only one who can decide on the use of units. At that time, the commander was the commander of the forward command post, Veroljub Zivkovic. In our army command rests on single command, and there is no duality of command. You can propose to the commander whatever you wish. The commander may adopt all of it, a part of it, or nothing. And the responsibility of the commander is indivisible. He has his authority. So if something is -- is a success he gets the credit. If something is a failure, that's his failure. Those are the elements that underlie relationships in our army, single command and indivisible responsibility, undivided responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But he, Zivkovic, could delegate to you the task of deciding how the units were going to be used in that action and delegate to you the authority to command that action, and that's what happened with regard to operation Sekac; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he approved that action. He approved the use of forces, which means that he was in agreement with everything that was written in the order. And my job, as an experienced officer, was to carry out the tasks with those units in the spirit of the order as written, to deal with any problems as they arise, and if I am unable to, then to seek his assistance or the assistance of a third party if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you have there referred to two pages from the Milosevic transcript. The first one you gave as 47872.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that should be 472, Your Honour. I must have misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may be. We may be part of the way there. And then you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or 482. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that now fits because you describe the next page as 483.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They are consecutive pages and that's the correct number, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, let me move to another topic for a moment. I want to talk about the Joint Command. You also were asked about this when you testified in the Milosevic trial, and this is at page 47518. Mr. Nice asked you what did you understand Joint Command to mean, and you said you understood it to mean a coordination body which from time to time spent time in Kosovo and Metohija. "And I'm referring to political organs that dealt with the questions of terrorism in Kosovo." And you mentioned the arrival of -- well, you said the arrival of General, I mean Mr. Sainovic Minic, Andjelkovic, and you also mentioned Lukic you say on page 47519: "So their mutual cooperation in terms of the realisation of these plans to break up terrorist groups in stages." Were you familiar with the plan that we've heard referred to sometimes as the five-stage plan for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard the plan existed, but I was not familiar with the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with regard to Joint Command, can you tell us the first time that you either heard that term used or saw it on a document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that term for the first time from Colonel Djakovic, then operations officer at the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Can you tell us approximately when that was you heard it from him, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would occasionally come from the forward command post to Pristina to have a day of rest, to see my family, just for one day and one night. It could have been June or July. I cannot tell you precisely, but it was warm. It was summertime. We wore short sleeves. And I met with Colonel Djakovic because we had rooms in the same hotel, and we met up and talked. That's all I can tell you. I cannot give you an a more precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it this conversation took place then in Djakovica -- or Pristina. I'm sorry, Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina. The Sloboda Hotel where we both had rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall how the topic first came up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Djakovic had just come from one meeting, and he said, "I had just been to a meeting at the MUP where I took notes," and he was invited to attend that meeting by General Pavkovic, and when he came back from that meeting he asked Pavkovic, in view of what had been agreed at the meeting, whether he needed to put it in a document. He asked for instructions, how to file it and record it. Pavkovic said that he should take a number from the register of the Pristina Corps and put it in our register. And when he asked about what to put in the signature, Pavkovic said, "Well, put Joint Command." And when he asked, "And who will sign?" Pavkovic said, "Just write 'Joint Command.'" Well, we bantered about that a little which is not important for this court, but that's how I heard for the first time of that term "Joint Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'm sorry, if you want to finish, it's time for our break but I'll let you finish your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say anyone who knows anything about the operational level of command will understand that this term simply doesn't wash in relation to what MUP and army officers did. In our lands, we have a person kum, who baptising children. We say God is in heavens and kum is on earth. So Pavkovic coined this term "Joint Command" and we were stuck with it just as one is stuck with the name that a kum gives to your child. In any case, the term "Joint Command" is incongruous for what they did. And that goes back to what I described earlier as the principles of our armies, single command and undivided responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. It's time for our break. We'll talk nor about it after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's convenient, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Lunchtime break this time, Mr. Kotur. Could you again leave with the usher, and we'll see you at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, when we broke you had just told us about your meeting with Colonel Djakovic and the discussion about Joint Command, and I understand from reading your Milosevic testimony at page 47524 apparently this was the second time that there had been a meeting in the corps, because you told us there in Milosevic that when Mr. Sainovic arrived to the area of Kosovo to gain an insight into the situation that prevailed, they had a meeting in the building of the MUP and there was General Lukic, Sainovic, and the corps commander Pavkovic. The second time they went to a meeting Colonel Djakovic, who was an operative at the time, was a direct participant. And as you explained to us he was invited to the meeting and took these notes. Was this the only time you had a conversation with Colonel Djakovic about the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I would not be asking about this, but to put this question this way is inaccurate. I don't know what he said in the Milosevic trial because Milosevic did not have professional counsel, and what he said there has a lesser weight in my eyes, but here he said that he talked to Djakovic once. He didn't mention Sainovic or the first and second meeting. So if something is asked, it should be asked in terms of whether, and if something is put to the witness it should be put accurately, because from Mr. Hannis's question, it transpires that it's something linked to Sainovic; and I haven't heard that. Let him rephrase the question. When did Djakovic first tell him about the Joint Command, and is that related in any way to Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic has been referred to already, excuse me, in this cross-examination, but probably, I think, by Mr. Hannis alone without anything being clarified although I'm speaking from vague recollection of this morning. Mr. Hannis, this question is a long question with a lot in it, and all that really matters is a bit at the end, which has nothing to do with Mr. Sainovic at all. Now, if you're going to be founding on the transcript in Milosevic, then it's got to somehow or other become an exhibit in this case or the words that were used there have to be accepted by the witness in the course of this examination. So it's for you to decide how you're going to deal with it, but all I would take from the question you've asked so far is whether he spoke to Mr. Djakovic on more than one occasion about the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Well, I would indicate that this transcript has an exhibit number, 5D1386. This witness was originally proposed as a 92 ter witness in connection with that transcript and then that was withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in Milosevic, at page 47523, Mr. Nice pointed out that you haven't explained how the thing is called the Joint Command, and we've been wrestling with this problem for months and we still haven't got an answer, and you said: "I will do so now. I will tell you. When Mr. Sainovic arrived to the area of Kosovo and Metohija to gain an insight into the situation that prevailed, they had a meeting in the building of the MUP. There was General Lukic, Sainovic, and the corps commander. What was it? Pavkovic. The second time they went to a meeting in the corps, Colonel Djakovic, who was an operative officer at the time. Since we lived together at the hotel I heard the story from him secondhand but he was a direct participant." Do you recall being asked that question and giving that answer during your testimony in Milosevic? First of all, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know about that first meeting attended by Sainovic, Lukic, and Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see it's secondhand piece of information. I believe that what you have read was said that way and recorded that way, but Djakovic told me that in one conversation, not several conversations. Whether that was really so or exactly so I cannot tell you with 100 per cent certainty, because what I know is secondhand. I believe I said even then that it was said in one conversation. I did not discuss the Joint Command with him several times. I remember that much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And it was in that one conversation. Did he also tell you that there was a second meeting which was the one he was invited to attend and at which he took notes? He also told you that at that one discussion; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, he told me that there was one meeting where Pavkovic went alone without any other officer from the corps command. And the second time he -- and how much time elapsed between the two, I don't know. I never knew that. And the second time Pavkovic went he took Djakovic with him to take notes. That's what I stated. I believe nothing else stands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did Djakovic show you the notebook in which he kept his notes of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He didn't show me. I never saw it, and I have no clue about these notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your continuing discussion about that with Mr. Nice in the Milosevic case, you went on to explain that Djakovic was told by General Pavkovic to find a number in the register and put it under a number, meaning the notes from the meeting. Did you ever see any of those documents with a Registry number from the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see those documents because I told you that from April 1998 until the end of October 1998 I was at the forward command post in Djakovica, and I had no occasion to see those documents or anybody's notebooks or to discuss it further with anyone else. I tried to be of some assistance to the Court to tell you who coined that term, who was the kum. That's the only context in which I mentioned it. Maybe there were other people who participated in coining that term. I first heard it from Djakovic and that's why I told you that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well you, did see at left one document that made reference to the Joint Command at the forward command post because we have that one that you and Jevtovic drafted; correct? That's Exhibit P1427. We can put that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, I didn't want to interrupt Mr. Hannis earlier, Colonel Kotur never said that. You heard his examination-in-chief, that Djakovic told him that General Pavkovic had told Djakovic to open a number in the register where he would put those notes. Instead he said that documents should be there, not notes. Unfortunately, we are now in a position where we have to split hairs. Those notes were misnamed by you minutes until I corrected that. Look at the transcript. Nobody mentioned notes. And now we seem to have it that General Pavkovic had told Djakovic to put the notes in the register of the corps. He said document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is -- which line in the evidence are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to find it. It's page 75, lines 6 to 10. That's where he speaks about notes. There is not a single corps which keeps notes in its register. It is said in the question. That's why the way Mr. Hannis is putting these questions is dangerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we're back to page 70 -- sorry, 47524. Does that actually contain that comment, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will -- I will read the quote so I'm precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in your testimony on 24 January 2006 at that page, you're telling us what Djakovic said about this, line 6: "He said Pavkovic invited him and told him: We're going to a meeting in the MUP to agree about actions and you will keep the record. So he did. Colonel Djakovic did keep a record. He asked Pavkovic: What shall we do with this record? Shall it be turned into an order, some sort of enactment? And Pavkovic told him: Find a number in the register and put it under a number."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, what's your objection in light of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, today he said those were notes, not record. It doesn't really matter that much. And that Pavkovic told him then to open a number for the ensuing order, because those notes had to be turned into an order. The register of a corps cannot contain notes. That much should be clear, I suppose. We are playing with interpretation. We are putting people -- like -- like with the words "operation" and "action." I ask about actions, the Prosecutor asks about operations for two years. Look at what Colonel Kotur said today, and I as St. Thomas, after whom I was named, believe my own eyes and ears than anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What interests Mr. Hannis at the moment is what Mr. Kotur said when he gave evidence on the 24th of January, 2006, and all he's doing is putting that to him to indicate the source of his information. I see nothing wrong in the way which his question has been framed so far and therefore the objection is repelled. You may have to start again though, Mr. Hannis. The quote we all know now. It may be simply a question of formulating -- reformulating the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, having heard what I just read about your testimony from Milosevic, do you recall? Is that how it happened in your discussion with Colonel Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall clearly having said those notes that Djakovic took in the MUP should be turned into a document, an order. Just to use this example in Djakovic. What Djakovic did in Pristina I did the same for that order when you asked me about it. I was at the meeting of MUP officers and our senior officers and kept notes, and those notes I used as a basis for writing that order. Axes, tasks per unit, et cetera. Those notes served as a basis for writing that document and Djakovic did that same thing. If that clarifies the matter enough. Because notes mean nothing. Everybody has their own way of keeping notes. I myself have difficulty reading my own notes after a certain passage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, that makes sense to me. Can I ask you in the example that you gave about how you took notes for that order that -- that you wrote, what happened to your original notes once the order was written? Are those original notes preserved anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those notes are kept in a service notebook. When it's filled completely, it is turned over to the archives and destroyed after one year. So the time they are kept in the archives is one year. After one year they are destroyed. So it is certainly not still kept after ten years. And that is a routine job, the destruction of those service notebooks. The only thing is that you have to turn it in once it's filled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you said earlier today about this meeting at page 70, line 14 you said: "And when he came back from that meeting he asked Pavkovic in view of what had been agreed at the meeting whether he needed to put in a document. He asked for instructions, how to file it and record it. Pavkovic said that he should take a number from the register from the Pristina Corps and put in our register. And when he asked what to put in the signature Pavkovic said, "Well, put Joint Command." And when he asked who will sign, Pavkovic said just write Joint Command." Am I right in understanding that he it is -- Djakovic goes to the meeting, he takes notes about the meetings, and then he comes back and writes up some official document that gets a Pristina Corps number and is filed in the Pristina Corps, whereas his notes remain separate and apart from that? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, 1427 is the document that I think you told us that you helped draft. Correct? Do you remember seeing this one and talking about it before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see this document before, and I wrote it and participated in its drafting, and you can best see that on the last page where initials are. MK is Milan Kotur, and Goran Jevtovic. And then you'll see "/GJ," which means that Goran Jevtovic actually printed it out on the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... page of both English and your language. I guess we have to go to the next to the last page of English for my next question. Colonel, under number 6 it's written: "Combat operations will be commanded by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija from the forward command post in Djakovica." Do you know why Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija was typed up in bold letters?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. You can see that Goran Jevtovic typed this. He typed "Report," and then "Commander." Commander shouldn't be written in such bold letters, bold script. I see that he muddled something in this text. I -- I don't know. I wouldn't know that, because I did not type it myself. I could not give you an explanation. I believe it's Goran's style to emphasise certain things, not necessarily because they were that important. And he did that arbitrarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In -- in your discussions about the Joint Command in 2006 when you testified in Milosevic, you didn't mention this document, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not mention it, and I didn't have it. I saw it for the first time here. I was even surprised a little when I saw my initials, and then I remembered the work done on this. Back then we did not have this document, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is -- this is dated the 10th of August, 1998. Do you remember when you and Jevtovic drafted -- drew it up? Was it the same day or did you do it the day before? Did it take a couple days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not need a couple of days to write this, but whether it was that same day or the next day, I really can't recall after ten years. Anything I would say would be guesswork and not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who -- whose idea it was to put "Joint Command" in item number 6? Did it come from you or Jevtovic or Pavkovic or who?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Pavkovic's idea. Whenever the MUP acted together with the army, it was labelled "Joint Command." We knew that these actions were linked up and agreed, but the command had nothing to do with it. Army commanders did not command the MUP or vice versa, nor did they submit reports to one another. That's why I said when somebody gives your child a name you don't like, you're stuck with it because kum is what God is in heaven. Now we are all struggling to explain this Joint Command, and it's really, really difficult because it doesn't have a single element of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How -- how -- well, I think you testified earlier that General Lazarevic, or I guess he was colonel then, was not at the forward command post at that time. How do you recall that he wasn't there that day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it only because of my initials here. If Colonel Lazarevic had been there, he would have done it as the more senior and more experienced officer, and my initials would not even be here. That's my recollection. And I would have noticed him in that group, because I know that later on I drafted this document without the benefit of his presence and his suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it you don't recall now where he would have been on the 9th or 10th of August, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, but I know he wasn't at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In talking about this document earlier, you told us that prior to writing it you attended some sort of coordination meeting with the MUP, and based on your notes, Pavkovic accepted it and then it was written up and Pavkovic signed it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officers of the MUP and officers of the army were all in Djakovica. Therefore, we didn't go to the MUP. They were both in Djakovica. That's where this action was considered, and it was decided to carry it out as I put it in this document. And I was at that meeting myself. I kept notes in order to be able to write this document on the basis of that. And at the meeting it was agreed which forces would participate, on which axes, what the tasks would be, what support would be given, how the tasks would be performed and how to deal with problems if they arise. At that meeting when everything is defined and coordinated, it is not a problem for me to write the order, and this is an order for our units that were to be engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you -- do you recall who scheduled a meeting and invited the people to come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I just saw all of them together when they were at the forward command post at the barracks in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you told us earlier today at page 30, line 17, that that was from the MUP, you believe Obrad Stevanovic, Vlastimir Djordjevic, and then you and Jevtovic and Pavkovic. Anyone else at that meeting that you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that, and I didn't say that. I think I said Obrad Stevanovic, General of the police. That's what I believe I said. You read a different name or, rather, last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I may have pronounced it badly, but that's the name I meant to read, Obrad Stevanovic. And Vlastimir Djordjevic, also known as Rodja. He was there too; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were talking about this, Mr. Bakrac asked you: "In taking this decision about coordination and support, did any -- and support to MUP forces, did any civilians take part?" And you started to answer and it's translated as "President of the municipality." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that the president of the municipality were -- was in Djakovica of the civilians, but not at the coordinating meeting but he just brought in some fruit that we ate. I don't know what the interpretation was, but that was the essence of it; so when I asked whether -- when I was asked whether any civilians were present there I said the president of the municipality who had brought in the fruit for us to eat, basket of fruit, but nobody else. There was no need for them to attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if -- you mentioned that if then Colonel Lazarevic had been there at the time this was written he would have written it himself and it wouldn't have your initials or Goran Jevtovic's initials on it; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initials of Goran Jevtovic would be there because he was the operations officer, and he typed those documents up, and he would have processed that. But not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what would it signify if there were an order like this that's signed by General Lazarevic and but there's no initials on it? Is it just the typist forgetting to put them on? What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would mean that the typist was not doing their job properly, because they were supposed to put the initials of the drafter and of the typist, but unfortunately it was not done in many cases. This was not something that was really focused on, but in office work it was the usual practice that was necessary to do so. You had to put the initials of the drafter and the typist, because you can see from these examples here in courtroom the purpose that it serves, because it refreshing your memory. Then you can say who drafted it after ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this -- this order, P1427, which seems to have primarily task for VJ units to support the MUP, you explained, I think -- yeah. You explained that that's when Joint Command got put in these orders. It was when it was a joint operation. When they were working together; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a group of officers from the police and the military planning this action together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One thing I note on here that we haven't seen on -- on several of the documents that I call Joint Command orders for action in combat, this one was sent to the MUP, wasn't it? You can see at the bottom of the page. Does it not indicate that a copy was sent to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a question related to this regarding the Reka action in late April 1999. We talked about that a bit, and I think it's your -- your evidence that as far as you know there wasn't any written order about that action. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, because our rules demand that there be no such plans for such an operation, and no special orders are required apart from those brief combat commands that are issued orally in the field, because at platoon and company level, those units never receive any written orders. They receive their orders directly in the field, and there is no need. I don't think that anyone ever wrote an order to a platoon or to a company except maybe in some exceptional circumstances when it was impossible to issue a task to a unit in the field, and then it was done in writing, but at this level it is not required in accordance with our rules. I'm talking about this level of deployment of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, would it be -- would it be unusual for a brigade commander to issue a written order from his level down to the units that you say were participating in this action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. These are also small units. And I don't know if you understand my correctly. Those units were already stationed there, and the only task that they had was to turn around some of their forces so that they don't -- they're no longer facing the Albanian border but the valley where the cleanup operations are being carried out. Because during the night and in some other circumstances this is the way they set up their security. They have the circular security to make sure that their battle order is not endangered by the terrorists. And this is the only order that those units received. I tried to emulate the chief of staff, the way in which he would have issued this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm not talking about the units that were blockading to try and avoid infiltration by -- by the KLA. I'm talking about those units of the VJ that were assisting the MUP in -- in mopping up and clearing that area. And we understood from Colonel Zivanovic that from the 125th there was a unit from the -- I think the 1st Motorised Battalion, and there was something that he referred to as the Volunteer Company. Were you aware that they were assisting in that mopping up part of the action?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is a mistake. General Zivanovic could not have said something like that, because the only units that participated in the search operations were 30 to 40 parachute troopers and 30 to 40 military police officers. These are the only units that participated in the search operations. As far as I know, all the rest of the VJ units were only preventing the terrorists from infiltrating the battle order of the units that were defending this area, and it had been going on for about a month already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is -- is the Rugovska gorge part of this area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Rugovska gorge is completely different area from Pec up towards Montenegro. That's the Pec-Cakor road. That's completely different axis, and this gorge extends from the west to the east, and this river runs north-south.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And part of the Reka area includes the village of Racaj, Pacaj, Seremet and Dobros, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Racaj, Pacaj, and Dobros. Yes. Those villages are part of this Reka area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we have a look at Exhibit P2024. Colonel, while this is coming up, I'll tell you it's a regular combat record dated 27 April 1999 from the 125th Motorised Brigade command. Let me ask you, would you in the forward command post receive these because I see it's addressed to both the Pristina Corps command post and the Djakovica command post. Did you receive the daily combat reports from those subordinate units operating in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that are subordinate to the commander of the forward command post in the Metohija area I already gave you the list those units, and among them is the 125th Brigade; and this brigade was duty-bound to send a copy of the report, combat report, that it is sending to the Pristina Corps command post in Pristina to send a copy to the forward command post, and this is what the 52nd and all the other subordinate units did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it your answer is yes, you would receive this kind of combat report from the 125th at the forward command post in April 1999; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operations officer did receive that, and Colonel Zivkovic read this report, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before we go to the second page, could you look down near the bottom. I think it's the next to the last paragraph. It starts out with: "During the day at 0800 hours, a column of Siptar civilians was formed on the following axis." Do you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the last sentence in that paragraph says: "We believe they want to pull out from the sector of operations of our forces in the general area of the Ramoc facility." First of all, can you tell us, if you know, what is the Ramoc facility?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who drafted this report. It comes from the 125th Brigade. If I knew the officers who drafted it then I would be able to tell you something more about it, but as to what you're asking me about, Ramoc is a village. It extends along the ridge of several kilometres. So there is no Ramoc feature, a physical feature in that sense, but there is the village of Ramoc, and the forces could have reached Ramoc, the village, only on the 27th, not before that, because that was the agreement regarding this action. And provided the units kept by this agreement, the agreement was that on the first day the line extending from Smonica --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Ramoc and Osehilja and Ose Pase would be reached. Now I can't recall the exact names because I don't have the map with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they were supposed to reach this line on the first day, and I don't know what this time means. This is all mixed up here. Maybe of some reservists wrote this because there were some reserve officers there who were in the command of this unit. So perhaps somebody who was not really very well-versed in how those reports are to be drafted actually did so. So you have the word "feature" or "facility" instead of the village. And then you have this 0800 hours. And they could not have reached Ramoc before the evening hours. And the next day they had to go through Ramoc, and this is like the most densely wooded area that you have to go through in order to get to Ramoc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The 0800 is referring to a column of civilians who are moving out of the area because your forces are carrying out actions in that general area. That's not confusing, is it? It's not talking about your forces moving out at 0800 from that axis. It's the civilians, the Siptar civilians who are moving.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It does say "civilians." I didn't understand your question when I gave you my answer. But Ramoc is not a facility. It's a village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have that answer. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to page 2 of the B/C/S. Colonel I want to ask you about something under item 2 on this page. The second sentence in English is translated as part of the forces is engaged in mopping up the terrain from Siptar terrorists in the general area of Reka in keeping with your decision." Doesn't that indicate that some VJ forces are mopping up in that area pursuant to a decision I take it of the Pristina Corps command? Doesn't say which ones but some; rights?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "A part of the forces is engaged in mopping up the terrain from Siptar terrorist forces in the general area of Reka in keeping with your decision." I think that this means that this police company that was subordinate -- it's a military police company from the 52nd Battalion. I think it was attached to the 100 -- or subordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade because of the problems it encountered at Kosare sector, and this parachute unit. And on the orders of the commander of the forward command post, those units were sent to mop up the terrain, and this order has to do with this mop-up operation, the military or those units, the mop-up operation, the military police and the parachute troops. You were talking to me about the volunteer group and so I got mixed up. I knew that those units did not participate in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, we're going to come to that in a minute, but to your recollection then the ones -- the VJ units participating in this were parts of the 52nd Military Police and part of the 63rd Parachute. Was it a brigade or a battalion? Whichever. Parts of the 52nd and the 63rd; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This police company was from the 52nd Military Police Battalion. It is a battalion that was under the command of the Pristina Corps command, and for the most part the forces of this battalion were deployed to secure the command post of the Pristina Corps regardless of its location, Grmija or some other place, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question, Mr. Kotur. Mr. Hannis, you're getting an awful lot of information that doesn't seem to be of assistance. I think you need more control over these questions.
