utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll make my best efforts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, were you trying to establish what the decision was that this refers to or is that not -- was that not part of the objective?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Part of the objective was to confirm whose decision that would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And have we got the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't think we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you read back to me what I read to you, that this was being done in keeping with your decision. In this context, when the 125th is writing to the Pristina Corps command, your decision means a decision of the Pristina Corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like you to put a ban on trick questions, because the reference is to the Pristina Corps and to the forward command post. This is what my learned colleague Mr. Hannis has said himself; and now he's trying to dupe the witness and tell him that this was sent to the Pristina Corps too, and we are now on the second page of this document, and on the front page you can see that this was a document that was sent both to the Pristina Corps command and to the forward command post in Djakovica and the witness has explained all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the witness was told that by Mr. Hannis at the outset. There is absolutely no question of a trick question here. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, did you understand my question? In this context when it says "pursuant" or "in keeping with your decision," who do you understand that to be referring to? Whose decision was it to carry out this mopping up of the terrain in the general Reka area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reference here is to the decision of the commander of the forward command post, that part of those units that were detached from the 125th Brigade would be used to mop up the Reka area, and this is how they explain this, in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, how do you know --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way I understand this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How do you know from reading this that it refers to someone in the forward command post as opposed to someone in the Pristina Corps command? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I know that Colonel Zivanovic had all those units -- or, rather, Zivkovic had all those units under his command and he was the only person who could issue orders to them. And Pristina Corps command couldn't do that because it had nothing to do with those units, because the corps commander in his order designated Colonel Zivkovic as the commander of the forward command post and subordinated to him all those units that were under the -- in this area under the forward command post. He was there until the end of the war and he was in command of all those forces. This is the essence of it. And this is why I said if I could see who drafted this document -- well, after all, the forward command post is part of the Pristina Corps command but it is just one part located in Djakovica. But this is part of the Pristina Corps command. It is not the command of some other corps, and this is why it was drafted in this manner. I think that now I understand much better what you were driving at. I understand much better your question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Kotur, you're being asked to slow down. So please speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not telling us that General Pavkovic -- or I guess in 1999 General Lazarevic, as commander of the Pristina Corps, had to defer to his deputy, had to defer to Zivkovic, if Lazarevic decided that he wanted to make an order about this? You talked to us about singleness of command. Lazarevic was the superior to Zivkovic; right? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So from reading this document, what -- what in here can you point to me that would say that this reference to your decision means Zivkovic instead of Lazarevic? There's nothing here in the written document that makes that clear, does it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is something, and it's called logic. It's in the manner in which command is exercised in our army. There is no reason. And I'm not trying to protect anyone. I'm just telling the truth. So please don't laugh. I have no reason to protect anyone to greater or lesser degree. I'm just trying to tell you that the command system is as follows: General Lazarevic didn't want to have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down when saying names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur I'm not going to ask you again to slow down. I've done it to the point where it's become really an offence to the Court for you to just ignore the constant requests of the interpreters. So please speak more slowly. I tell you for the last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may assist. Mr. Kotur, please look at the transcript in front of you and don't open your mouth for as long as you can see that the letters are being typed up, and that's all. And we'll have no problems. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I was facing the Prosecutor, and I did not monitor the transcript. Your instruction is taken, your warning is taken, and I do apologise. I'm not doing this deliberately, as a sign of contempt. General Lazarevic had no reason to poll individually several brigade commanders and to issue individual orders to all of them. When he had his deputy who was the commander of the forward command post and if anything needed to be done he issued only his orders only to him. So there was no need for him to call Colonel Zivanovic, who was not at the forward command post at any rate. He was up there at the Kosare region where his unit had its battle disposition, and he couldn't even get him on the phone during the entire day. When he had the simple option of calling the forward command post and ordering his chief of staff to do something, if that's what he, Lazarevic, wanted to be done. So that was the way in which we exercise command in our army. So that's one thing. Secondly, it was difficult to establish communications from Pristina with each and every unit that was located or stationed here in Metohija defending the axes leading from Albania into the Kosovo and Metohija area. So the only communication that was maintained was the one with his forward command post in Djakovica. When I said logic, that is the essence of the command system, and I can claim with 100 per cent certainty, 101 per cent, that Lazarevic could not simply get Zivanovic on the phone and order this. And you had Zivanovic here yesterday and he was in a position to tell you so. I don't know what he told you, but that was the only thing that he could have told you, and that's that the chief of staff -- that the chief of staff, Zivkovic, ordered this rather than Colonel Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I have to take issue with your logic, Colonel. Let's look at Exhibit P1966 first of all. And while it's coming up, let me ask you. Are you saying because these units, these subordinate elements of the 125th were operating in the area of the forward command post Lazarevic couldn't or wouldn't or needn't be bothered with sending them instructions? Is that what you're saying? And he left that all to the forward command post all the time? That's not what you're claiming, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me just say the following: What I'm saying is that from the moment the forward command post was established, from that point on I'm not aware that Lazarevic commanded special units let alone small units such as a police platoon or a parachute platoon. The forward command post was established on the 13th or 14th of April, 1999, as I said. Up to that point in time while there was the command group with Jevtovic and others, they didn't have the right to command units by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And no one could authorise them to do so because they were not up to the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have a look at this document on the screen in front of you. You'll see it's dated the 22nd of March, 1999. It's captioned "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, strictly confidential number 455-56.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's probably a misinterpretation, because the witness was told it's the 27th. In the transcript it's correct, but the witness heard the date 27th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document is in fact the 22nd of March, 1999. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is an order to rout and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in the Malo Kosovo area. Colonel, I will tell you that it includes some task for Battle Group 4 of the 125th. Have you ever seen this document before? Did you see it in preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'll tell you, this one is unsigned. It just has the typed name "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija" on the last page, and it says that the operations will be commanded by the Joint Command. But note that number on the front. It's 455-56. And from other witnesses we've heard evidence that that is a number, a register number, associated with the Pristina Corps. Would you agree with that, the 455 series?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a lapse of ten years, it's hard for me to say either yes or no. I have no idea what the serial numbers were in the Pristina Corps logbook. I wasn't in the operative department or in the Registry office. It wasn't my job, so I'm not familiar with that. It's easy to establish, however, if the logbook is still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me show you the next exhibit, P1967. And, Colonel, while that's coming up I'll tell you that this is also dated the 22nd of March, 1999, and it appears to be related to the one you just looked at for a couple reasons. It has the number 455-56/1, and it's called "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP and breaking up the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo." Would you agree with me that this appears to be related to the one that you just looked at because of the number and the fact at that says "Amendment"? That's logical, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical, and I would agree that this is an annex to that document because it says "/1". So it is an addendum to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page then of this document. And this -- this amendment, which was titled "Joint Command," like the document which it amends, is signed by General Lazarevic. You see -- recognise his signature and stamp there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it has tasks for the 125th, and we see on the delivery information that among others it was sent to the 125th Motorised Brigade. Now, isn't that contrary to what you were telling me before? Here's General Lazarevic issuing an order to 125th Brigade, Battle Group 4, which I believe is operating in the area within the forward command post area of coverage?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no logic in this. I explained to you from when the forward command post began to function. At that time, the forward command post was still not functioning, and the 125th Brigade had not yet taken up its positions to defend the axes going from Albania to Kosovo. So the manner of exercise and command differed before and after that point in time. THE PROSECUTOR:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Help me with that. When -- when was -- first of all, in 1998 when was the forward command post set up in Kosovo, the forward command post for the Pristina Corps, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the second half of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was it disbanded or when did it cease to function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the 11 -- I think sometime November or December 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And -- and then when did it get reconstituted? What was the date it started in 1999, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you. After --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I just need the date. Can you just tell me the date?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th or 14th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another exhibit then.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In between was the command group. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I heard your testimony about that earlier. So the 13th or 14th of April. Could we look at P1878. Now, I understand from your earlier testimony that -- that for you there was no Joint Command in the sense of a body with command authority; right? That's your position.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these documents that are entitled Joint Command with orders for combat actions or operations are really coming from the Pristina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: P1878 is dated the 15th of April, from the Joint Command, and it's an order to break up and destroy Siptar terrorists in the Rugova sector. You'll see it seems to be a pretty small operation. It if we could go to item number 5, which is page 3 of the English, and it's the very bottom of page 2 of the Serbian B/C/S. There's a task for the 125th, the 2nd Battalion of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade. Do you see that? And if you want to go on to the next --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go on to the next page you'll see what area it's talking about. Do you recognise those villages or the area that's described?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not really familiar with Rugovska Klisura, but I can see that it deals with that. Rugovska gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And isn't this an example of an order after the forward command post had been reconstituted or reset up? After that date we have an order from the Pristina Corps command for an element of the 125th. Isn't that contrary to what you told us before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this question then: Would you describe this as a joint action or is this a separate army task or a separate MUP task? Can you tell by reading it? I can give you a hard copy if you want to look at the whole thing, in fairness to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here one can see that at the command post of the Pristina Corps an action was agreed on to be conducted jointly by the MUP and the army with a view to routing and destroying Siptar terrorist forces in the general area of mount Rugovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from what you testified to earlier, that is consistent with my understanding what you said for joint actions those are the ones that needed to have this language about Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, could you repeat your question? I was looking at the document and I didn't quite follow. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. I understood from what you told us earlier that for those joint actions that involved both MUP and VJ, those orders needed to contain this language about the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command all the forces, and that's in this document. So that's consistent with what you told us before; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are no elements of command here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's -- that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see in the heading where it says "Joint Command," and then it says "Pristina Corps command post," under 11 it says "Peacetime location," in item 11, and I don't see to whom all this was sent, because a document in this form cannot be sent to the units. The units have to receive other documents along with this, maps and so on, because as far as I was able to see here you indicated 125th Brigade and the 2nd Battalion of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade. So a battalion from another unit is being sent there to be engaged here. And up here it says Joint Command, and then where it says "Command" it says only the command of the Pristina Corps. It's very hard to find my way around here. My understanding is that the Pristina Corps command was in command of its own forces, as always, and why it says Joint Command up there, probably because MUP forces are mentioned in here. And why it doesn't say that there will be a Joint Command, I really don't know, because there are documents where there's a Joint Command in the heading or in the signature or only in the signature or only in the command elements. So it's mentioned in one place and not the other. I really don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. Look at the first page of that document. At the top it says "Joint Command"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And look at the last page. Does it not have the typed signature "Joint Command"? "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in item number 13, the second sentence, does it not say: "The Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command all forces from the Pristina sector during the conduct of combat operations"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says that in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the point I was trying to get to is I understood from your earlier testimony when these documents had that kind of thing in it about Joint Command, that meant this was going to be a joint action between the VJ and MUP. Isn't that what you told us before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I don't know if -- if you're aware. We've had evidence in this case that this particular order, number 455-148, was brought to the attention of General Ojdanic, the -- the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, and that he actually wrote a document that was called "Suggestions." Were you aware of that from following this trial or in your preparation for testifying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you're getting no transmission. Are you aware that this document, number 455-148, is an order that came to the personal attention of General Ojdanic, the chief of the Supreme Command Staff, and that he actually wrote a document called "Suggestions," making some suggestions about how this might be done differently? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't pay attention. And if the document was there somewhere, I didn't pay attention to it, because I did not participate in any Joint Command except for once in Djakovica at the forward command post. So I don't know anything about it. And as I told you, when something erroneous creeps in it's never put right. And now I cannot assist much regardless of my experience. All I know is that this title cannot hold water. It's not tenable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand your position, and I take it that even though I've mentioned to you that this came to the attention of General Ojdanic and he wrote "Suggestions," he didn't right to the subordinate units and say, "Disregard any orders from a Joint Command because I'm in charge," he wrote "Suggestions" which to me suggests he recognises the Joint Command and is sort of deferring to it. Isn't that how it seems when the chief of the Supreme Command Staff knows about a Joint Command and doesn't do anything except make suggestions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this witness said he didn't know what this was about at all, that he hadn't seen the document and that he didn't know what my learned friend is talking about and now my learned friend is asking him to draw conclusions on documents he hasn't seen and doesn't know what they're about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If I could just add my comment, Your Honour. I think Mr. Hannis is making a submission here, not really asking a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question was spurred by the answer where he said: "All I know is that this title cannot hold water. It's not tenable."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. What did you mean by that, Mr. Kotur, when there is a document in which General Ojdanic appears to have written suggestions about the instructions which were contained in P1878, the document you've been looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Bonomy, I don't have that document. I have the order on the routing of forces in Rugova. That's on my screen, and that's what I'm holding. So I don't know what you're referring to. I'm really not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want to show the witness the document, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'd like to but I don't think I put Exhibit P1487 on my notification list, but I would -- if it would assist him, I'd like to show it to him, and I'll listen to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I believe you're being invited to by Mr. Bakrac so that he's fully informed. Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that a document that has not been announced should not even be shown, but counsel didn't show it. He tried to discuss it with the witness precisely because it had not been announced or disclosed in advance and I think we have strict rules here which apply to us also when a document is not announced it cannot be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The problem that's been created here is that an answer was given to question that was not objected to and that answer was that the use of the expression, "suggestions," in the context was untenable militarily, as I understand the position, and Mr. Hannis has tried to explore that to enable the witness to explain what he meant by untenable then it's only right he should have the -- what do you --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the witness did not say that the suggestions were untenable. What he said was this was actually about whether the Joint Command existed or not, and he said that the Joint Command was untenable in military terms. So he was not commenting on the suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't agree with that interpretation. It's open to more than one interpretation, that answer. If you take the one you've just given but I certainly would not have taken that interpretation from the English translation. You'll be able to make submissions about that and the witness will be able to explain himself on that. So we'll allow Mr. Hannis to let him see the document and then see if he can assist us further in where this document fits into the command structure that he's been so helpfully exploring with Mr. Hannis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if we could bring up on e-court Exhibit P1487.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you'll see this is dated the 17th of April, from the Supreme Command Staff, and you can see on your B/C/S -- or your Serbian version the signature and seal of General Ojdanic at the bottom. Okay. And you'll see it's to the 3rd Army command, commander personally, and there's a link to Kosovo and Metohija Joint Command order number 455-148 of 15 April. That -- that one you have on the desk in front of you. Now, do you want to take a minute to read the whole thing before I ask my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to time some read it, because this is the first time that I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. Take your time and let us know when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this -- the way I read this, it seems the highest uniformed individual in the army is giving some kind of deference to this body called Joint Command, because he is writing suggestions, suggesting for example, in number 3, delaying the task to the 19th of April. Now, doesn't that suggest to you that the Joint Command is somebody, some organ, that has some substantial say in VJ combat actions for the supreme -- for the chief of the supreme command staff to be responding to its order this way?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what made Mr. Ojdanic to draft this in this manner, but I don't believe that the Joint Command staff that you're talking about, that he is showing this kind of respect to be treating this suggestion in this manner for a very simple reason, because the war started. The supreme commander of the Command was Mr. Milosevic, and Ojdanic was the first person next to him and the most competent one in the professional sense. And if any orders were to be issued to the Joint Command or if General Ojdanic believed that orders should be issued, he would not have couched them as suggestions. He would have just ordered that, and he would not be deferring to this command in any way. So I can't read it in this manner. I can't understand it that way. As for the suggestions, I think that his organs estimate was better, that he saw that and he perhaps was not sure whether he had missed something, and now he didn't want to belittle his generals, his colleagues, telling them that they did not plan this operation in the proper manner. So he is not issuing an order but is just making those is suggestions in this document. This is the only way in which I can interpret this document. I may be wrong, but this is the first time that I see this document. This is my thinking at this point in time. And based on what I knew, I never heard about the existence of this Joint Command during the war. I did see at the forward command post and I can see now from those documents that it apparently did exist; but this may have been for the very simple reason because the MUP was not subordinate to the VJ and because there were those joint coordinated actions this term "Joint Command" started to be used. I was not at the Pristina Corps command post, so I couldn't really comment on it. I didn't even hear about the reasons why this was written or about the existence of maybe some problems at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please Colonel stop --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- That would lead them to use those titles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're getting beyond my questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kotur, is the form of this document,"suggestions," something you're familiar with in the course of your work in the VJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, let me move on to something else if I may. And one thing you said in Milosevic at page 47525, when you and Mr. Nice were talking about the Joint Command; and you said that the subordinate commanders such as Jelic, Delic, could never obtain a document which would say "Joint Command." If Jelic or Delic received any documents, they needed to receive documents signed by the corps commander, not like this without any signature at all or with just "Joint Command" at the bottom. Do you recall giving that answer to a question by Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that still your position today?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still maintain that this document alone, without anything could not have had any effect. They would have had to receive another document indicating that this was from the corps command. So this document alone, I still maintain that it shouldn't have come in. Of course all kinds of things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you Exhibit P2113. This is a document from the 125th Motorised Brigade. It's dated the 7th of July, 1998. And have you seen this before based on what you're able to read on the screen right now?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I didn't have an opportunity. Perhaps during the war, I think, I might have seen it. It's 1998. But I didn't see it now during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. This comes from Colonel Zivanovic to his subordinates, and you'll see item number 1 under the order says: "I prohibit the execution of any operations by units and formations without the approval of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija and my own approval." Do you read that there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He and above that in the introductory paragraph he has written: "Pursuant to the order of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Strictly confidential. Number 1104-6, of 6 July 1998. "I hereby order that ban on operations without the approval of the Joint Command," and I will tell you that he testified that this was his order and that he wrote it that way. And would you agree with me that a subordinate when passing on an order from a superior will incorporate the language of the order that he has received from his superior? That's standard practice in the VJ, isn't it? If you got an order from -- from the commander of the forward command post that you were passing on, or from General Lazarevic, in 1999, you, in passing it on, would incorporate the language in the order you got; right? You're not allowed to change it.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That's how it would be done. The first part would not be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on his answer to the same effect to that question, I then ask him if he agreed then even though he did not have a copy of 1104-6 in front of him, he agreed that it must have been entitled "Joint Command," otherwise he wouldn't have written that in his order to his subordinates. That makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what Dragan told you, then it probably is how it was. We at the forward command post in Djakovica in 1998, we were dealing with completely different matters, so I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, at the forward command post weren't you also occasionally dealing with the Joint Command or actions directed by the Joint Command? You wrote P1427 from the 10th of August, which makes reference to the Joint Command being in command of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOTUR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Kotur.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no problem with the questions asked by Mr. Hannis or, that is, if he asked his questions one by one. Now he asked three questions, one, two, three. So now I'm just wondering which one, whether he had contacts with the Joint Command, that's one question. Whether he had any contact with the documents of the Joint Command. That's the second question. And now we have the third question about the order. So could he just ask his questions one by one and then we'll be fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript, Your Honour. I see one question and one statement. But perhaps it's a good time to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your question is what? Just let's complete this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is, Colonel, weren't you also occasionally dealing with the Joint Command on actions directed by the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that's where the problem arises because your question really is you wrote P1427 from the 10th of August which makes reference to the Joint Command being in command of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's just a statement. He's already said that and agreed with that. It's not a question. That's just a reminder, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's a difference between dealing with actions directed by documents which refer to the Joint Command and dealing with the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's the point Mr. Fila's making.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be a good time to break then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kotur, we have to terminate our proceedings for today at this stage and resume tomorrow when you will require to return. Tomorrow we have to sit in the afternoon, so you need to be here to resume your evidence at 2.15 tomorrow. Could you now please leave the courtroom with the usher. Or, sorry, in Courtroom III is that tomorrow? Yes, Courtroom III tomorrow, a different courtroom as well at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
